Hugging Face ❤️ TorchTPU: TPUs, Natively

📖 0% read
💡 Key Takeaways
  • If you ever tried to run PyTorch on a TPU, you probably ported your code to torch_xla, or you ended up having to learn JAX.
  • In a recent development, TPU stands for Tensor Processing Unit.
  • TPUs are available on Google Cloud, from a single chip up to pods of thousands of chips.
📑 Quick Jump: 1. Overview • 2. Key Details • 3. Closing Notes

If you ever tried to run PyTorch on a TPU, you probably ported your code to torch_xla, or you ended up having to learn JAX. With TorchTPU, a native PyTorch backend, TPU is now just another device. It opens up native support of TPU in the Hugging Face ecosystem. Transformers, Diffusers and Kernels run natively on TPU. Pick a model from the Hub, send it to "tpu", and you're done.

In a recent development, TPU stands for Tensor Processing Unit. TPUs are Google's own AI accelerators. They are chips built for one job: the matrix math that neural networks spend most of their time on. Google has been designing them for about ten years, and uses them to train and serve its own models, including Gemini.

TPUs are available on Google Cloud, from a single chip up to pods of thousands of chips. They shine when you need a lot of compute, for training or for serving at scale.

Sources indicate that the catch has always been software. The TPU stack grew up around TensorFlow and JAX, and PyTorch customers had to work harder to get in.

Until now, running PyTorch on TPUs meant going through PyTorch/XLA (torch_xla). It worked, but it had its quirks. Tensors were lazy (the tensors, not you), so your code didn't always run when you thought it did. Small changes could trigger graph recompilations, and debugging was hard to reason about.

To make life easier, we built Optimum TPU. It gave Hugging Face models inference and training support on TPUs. Now that TorchTPU brings native support, Optimum TPU is not required anymore to run Hugging Face models with Transformers and Diffusers.

Industry observers note that torchTPU adds TPU as a fresh backend to PyTorch. You write regular PyTorch code. It comes with Pallas kernels tuned for TPUs, support for distributed training, and a torch.compile integration for when you want more speed. Installing it on a TPU VM takes one command:.

The extra index gives you the CPU build of torch. Without it, pip pulls the much bigger CUDA build, which you don't need on a TPU.

Transformers v5 was built around one idea: be the source of truth for model definitions, so they can run anywhere. "Anywhere" now includes TPUs. To load a model on a TPU, pass device_map="tpu". That's it.

Sources indicate that the model runs in eager mode by default. You can also use torch.compile for better performance, or run it in a distributed setup.

TPU is now a first-class device in Diffusers. For prototyping or debugging, eager mode only needs pipe.to("tpu"). For deployment, compiled mode adds one compile call. Your pipelines and code stay the same, and there's no TPU fork to maintain.

The first call compiles, and every call after that with the same image size reuses the graph.

Recent findings suggest that models too substantial for one chip? Pass a TensorParallelConfig to from_pretrained and the transformer is sharded across chips as it loads, so the full model never has to fit in one place. Many popular pipelines support it out of the box, and the ones that don't are just a tp_plan away. The Diffusers TPU guide has the full recipe.

Here are some examples run on a Cloud TPU v6e-4:.

TP=4 (each model split across four chips) · bf16 · batch 1.

It has been revealed that the Kernels Hub has ready-to-use TPU kernels. Load one with the Kernels library and give your model a speed boost.

TPU kernels are written in Pallas, which gives you low-level control over the hardware. You can also bring in kernels from the Tokamax library. Here is a ragged-dot kernel from Tokamax plugged into a Mixture-of-Experts model:.

The bigger the batch, the bigger the win. At batch size 64, decoding is 21.5× faster on Qwen3-30B-A3B and 12.8× faster on Gemma 4 26B-A4B.

Decode throughput on a TPU v6e-8, Hub kernel vs. the default implementation.

In a recent development, we're continuously improving TPU support in transformers by running the library test suite. We are working to add a nightly CI on TPU and make the results available in the (transformers dashboard)[https://huggingface.co/spaces/transformers-community/transformers-ci-dashboard].

Sources indicate that the Transformers CI dashboard, with TPU results next to other accelerators. Work in progress!

It's not all green yet, and we're fine with that. Of the tests that run on TPU, 96.5% pass. Every failure we find becomes a small repro script and an glitch on the TorchTPU repo. So far we have reported 34 concerns, and 19 are already fixed. Running on TPU also caught a few bugs in Transformers itself, like in StaticCache and the Qwen3 tensor-parallel prepares. We fixed those upstream.

If something breaks on TPU, we want to find out before you do.

According to recent reports, TPUs are no longer a side quest for PyTorch people. Install TorchTPU, grab a model from the Hub, and send it to "tpu".

According to recent reports, we can't wait to see what you build 🤗. If you hit a problem, open an matter and tell us about it.

Tech Report: From Intent to Autonomous Action: Governing AI Agents in the Enterprise

📅 19 Nov 2026 | ⏱️ 5 min read (978 words, 📚 Deep Dive) | Source: Unite

⏱️ ~5 mins left to finish
📖 0% read
💡 Key Takeaways
  • Industry observers note that an instruction such as “restore service” sounds straightforward until an AI agent must decide what it authorizes.
  • According to recent reports, governance belongs inside the product because it determines which responsibilities an organization can confidently delegate.
  • Industry observers note that putting those boundaries into practice requires a consistent way to govern how agents act.
📑 Quick Jump: 1. Overview • 2. Key Details • 3. Closing Notes

Industry observers note that an instruction such as “restore service” sounds straightforward until an AI agent must decide what it authorizes. Restarting an application, changing a configuration, and provisioning infrastructure may all support that objective, but each carries different consequences. As agents move from recommending actions to executing them, organizations need an explicit connection between business intent and operational authority.

According to recent reports, governance belongs inside the product because it determines which responsibilities an organization can confidently delegate. An agent that can complete a task reliably, within agreed boundaries and with evidence of its actions, offers a stronger foundation for enterprise adoption than one whose authority remains ambiguous. The architectural challenge is to make those boundaries part of how the system operates.

Industry observers note that putting those boundaries into practice requires a consistent way to govern how agents act. An agentic control plane can provide this foundation by connecting agent identity, approved capabilities, policy enforcement, memory controls and execution oversight across existing enterprise systems. It establishes who requested an action, what authority supports it, which resources it can affect and how its outcome will be verified.

Here are three practical guidelines we recommend for governing AI agents in the enterprise:.

Every agent should have an identifiable owner, a defined purpose and permissions appropriate to its task. This aligns with the NIST AI Risk Management Framework, which treats governance as a continuous function across the AI lifecycle. For agents, that principle must extend to the moment an action changes an enterprise system. When one agent delegates to another, those boundaries should remain intact.

According to recent reports, capability discovery requires similar discipline: an approved catalogue should describe each tool’s purpose, inputs, outputs, permitted environments and potential side effects. Discovering a tool does not confer permission to execute it, so authorization must be checked when an action is attempted. OWASP’s Excessive Agency guidance reinforces this distinction through recommendations to limit functionality and permissions and enforce authorization in downstream systems.

In a recent development, consider an illustrative service recovery workflow in which an agent investigates an application slowdown and proposes restarting a component. Policy permits access to approved telemetry, while a production restart requires evidence that redundancy is healthy and approval from the service owner. These conditions turn a broad instruction into a bounded operational decision.

If an approved recovery tool exists, the agent can prepare a request using that capability. Where none exists, it may help create a script, runbook, input schema and tool descriptor, translating operational intent into a proposed capability that others can inspect. This is the practical value of agentic tool coding: agents can contribute to the machinery of operations as well as use it.

It has been revealed that generating that machinery, however, should not automatically make it executable in production. A proposed capability needs an independent release process with accountable ownership, security checks, version control and tests covering invalid inputs, excessive scope, partial failures and repeated execution. Agent-generated tests can contribute evidence, but independent validation should establish whether the capability meets its operational requirements before it enters the approved catalogue.

Execution boundaries should then constrain resource scope, network access, duration and spending, with any required approval attached to the specific action, target and version. Recovery arrangements deserve equal attention because some changes can be rolled back, while others require compensating actions or cannot be undone. Each capability should make those limitations clear and provide operators with a tested way to suspend further execution.

Sources indicate that memory introduces another governance responsibility because retained observations can influence future decisions long after their original context has changed. Organizations should define what agents may store, how long information remains available and which access boundaries apply, supported by provenance and correction mechanisms. A remembered permission must never become standing authority, and outdated operational knowledge should not silently guide latest actions.

Meaningful oversight depends on evidence that connects the original request, applicable policy, approval, tool version, execution result and subsequent verification. Human reviewers need enough context to assess the proposed change, its uncertainty and its recovery options without being overwhelmed by unnecessary detail. To support that oversight, escalation should follow defined conditions, such as conflicting observations or an unfamiliar system state, rather than rely solely on an agent’s expressed confidence.

In a recent development, IT leaders should begin with a narrow workflow and expand authority as operational evidence supports it, measuring successful outcomes alongside exceptions, recovery time, policy violations and oversight effort. These measures help determine whether an agent is ready for greater responsibility and where additional safeguards or testing are needed.

Recent findings suggest that the opportunity is to make delegation repeatable, with each approved capability establishing what an agent can do, under which conditions and with what accountability. That discipline can strengthen resilience and efficiency while giving organizations a defensible basis for granting greater autonomy. The biggest takeaway is this: governance earns its place in the product by making that progression possible.

Sources indicate that casey Kindiger is the Founder and CEO of Droma (formerly Grokstream), an enterprise AI company advancing predictive and agentic operations, and a serial entrepreneur who previously founded Resolve Systems. With more than 25 years in enterprise technology, a decade leading applied AI/ML research teams, and a master’s degree in Psychology & Neuroscience of Mental Health from King’s College London, he brings a distinctive perspective on how human cognition can inform the development of more capable, trustworthy AI systems.

Tech Report: Producing Healthy Code with Artificial Intelligence Costs Fewer Tokens

⏱️ ~4 mins left to finish
📖 0% read
💡 Key Takeaways
  • InfoQ Homepage News Producing Healthy Code with Artificial Intelligence Costs Fewer Tokens.
  • Nov 19, 2026 4 min read.
  • It has been revealed that agentic AI can speed up velocity, but the gains vanish within months as code complexity grows.
📑 Quick Jump: 1. Overview • 2. Key Details • 3. Closing Notes

InfoQ Homepage News Producing Healthy Code with Artificial Intelligence Costs Fewer Tokens.

Nov 19, 2026 4 min read.

It has been revealed that agentic AI can speed up velocity, but the gains vanish within months as code complexity grows. In his presentation on AI-friendly code at GOTO Copenhagen, Adam Tornhill showed that healthy code makes AI perform better and costs fewer tokens. Safeguarding means keeping code health high through agentic refactoring, with an MCP supplying code health data, so AI can maintain the code it generates.

It has been revealed that developing software with agents is significantly harder than writing code manually, Tornhill argued. But with agentic AI, they can complete tasks two to three times faster, he added. It also helps them unblock themselves and reduces coordination needs.

Tornhill mentioned a study done on 1000+ open-source projects which demonstrated that with AI, velocity went up during the first few weeks, but after two months the velocity gains were fully canceled out due to a massive increase in code complexity:.

AI operates in a self-harm mode, often writing code it cannot reliably maintain later.

It has been revealed that code health measures how easy code is to understand, change, and maintain. Research done on human coding (before AI) shows that if you have healthy code, you can be up to 10x faster than someone who works on similar problems in unhealthy code, Tornhill mentioned. The defect risk is reduced 15 times, and code reviews go twice as quickly, he added.

It has been revealed that building a prototype was never the hard problem in software; 95% of the costs for any software project come after the first release. This is where code quality, maintainability, and architecture start to matter, Tornhill said.

Recent research shows that large language models perform consistently better in healthy code. AI won’t generate perfect code; if we want to survive in the Agentic age, we need to focus on safeguarding, Tornhill stated.

In a recent development, the average codebase has a code health of 5.15, where AI-friendly code starts at 9.5. Technical depth is a bottleneck for enterprise adoption of agentic coding; what’s needed is an agentic refactoring, Tornhill argued. Claude can be used to fix code health issues, but only to a certain extent:.

It has been revealed that as a best-case scenario, an agent can fix roughly 50% of the code health issues for lower-health code. Once the code health improves, the AI performance drops sharply, and Claude can only correctly refactor 20% of the code. AI tends to become conservative, doing small changes that don’t really move the needle on code quality.

In a recent development, adding an MCP with code health data can lead to a 90%-100% fix rate, Tornhill said. Agentic refactoring turned out to be a predictable and mechanical process at scale, where AI was capable of doing codebase-specific refactorings.

Healthy code is also financially viable code, with healthy code, you can do things with 40% to 45% fewer tokens, Tornhill mentioned.

According to recent reports, by refactoring code, modularizing it and making it healthy, we can also reduce organizational friction, Tornhill said. Code quality at the module level is a largely solved problem with the automation we now have. Scaling AI friendliness to the design and architectural level is the next big challenge, he concluded.

InfoQ interviewed Adam Tornhill after his talk.

InfoQ: How can we measure code health?

Adam Tornhill: Code Health is a multifacetted concept, so we need to combine multiple metrics. We’ve found that it works best when combining measures from three levels of software design:.

InfoQ: How do you safeguard AI-generated code?

Industry observers note that tornhill: Safeguarding needs to happen at multiple levels, and all safeguards need to be completely automated in an agentic context. Examples of concrete safeguards include linting, code coverage, mutation testing to ensure your tests actually test, and higher-level metrics like Code Health. In practice, these safeguards are exposed to agents as local MCP servers or command-line tools.

InfoQ: How can we do refactoring at scale with agents?

According to recent reports, tornhill: The main steps are to establish a baseline, build a safety-net for behavior, and provide a feedback loop to the agents refactoring the code. The whole process is highly iterative.

Presented by: David Iparraguirre - Senior Product Marketing Manager at Datadog, and Jessica Yang - Product Manager at Datadog.

Latest Update: Profiling TorchNeuron (Part 1): System-level profiling on AWS Trainium.

📅 21 Oct 2026 | ⏱️ 7 min read (1303 words, 📚 Deep Dive) | Source: Hugging Face

⏱️ ~7 mins left to finish
📖 0% read
💡 Key Takeaways
  • According to recent reports, many ML practitioners have some intuition about how to make models run fast, but fewer know how to analyze why a model is slow.
  • It has been revealed that this post starts from scratch and assumes no prior profiling experience.
  • Before you profile a workload, it helps to understand how Neuron integrates with PyTorch.
📑 Quick Jump: 1. Overview • 2. Key Details • 3. Closing Notes

According to recent reports, many ML practitioners have some intuition about how to make models run fast, but fewer know how to analyze why a model is slow. In Part 1 of this series, you will learn how to systematically analyze inference performance and identify where the time is spent.

It has been revealed that this post starts from scratch and assumes no prior profiling experience. The walkthrough uses AWS Trainium, a purpose-built AI chip for deep learning training and inference workloads, and TorchNeuron, its open source native PyTorch backend. TorchNeuron supports standard PyTorch workflows on Trainium, including eager execution, torch.compile, and standard PyTorch APIs, with minimal code changes. Additionally, TorchNeuron integrates with Neuron Kernel Interface (NKI) to enable custom operators and performance optimization for Trainium hardware. By the end, you should know:.

Before you profile a workload, it helps to understand how Neuron integrates with PyTorch.

According to recent reports, the Neuron backend uses PyTorch's PrivateUse1 extension point. This mechanism lets an accelerator integrate with the framework without adding a dedicated dispatch key such as cuda. The torch_neuronx package works with upstream PyTorch to register Neuron as a native backend for PyTorch code. For details about this extension mechanism, see Facilitating New Backend Integration by PrivateUse1.

You use two objects to profile a Neuron workload:.

In a recent development, the modes parameter selects the data streams to capture, such as device instructions and runtime traces. The capture_enabled_for_nc parameter selects the NeuronCores to trace. Setting correlate_device_time=True propagates device time from the trace into the key_averages() table, where you can compare CPU and Neuron device time. For the complete parameter reference and available ProfileMode values, see the NeuronConfig Profile Modes documentation.

Sources indicate that neuron Explorer is a browser-based viewer for the system trace, device timeline, and per-engine breakdown. You can access it through an SSH tunnel or the Visual Studio Code extension. In this post, you use Explorer to confirm what key_averages() reports numerically and inspect what happens between dispatches.

It has been revealed that after profiling, the output directory contains the system trace and, when you capture device data, matched .neff and .ntff files. The Neuron Executable File Format (NEFF) contains the compiled Neuron executable, while the matching NTFF contains its hardware instruction trace. The files share a numeric hash that identifies them as a pair. To open the profile in Neuron Explorer, upload the complete output directory for a system or combined profile. For a device-only profile, upload the matching .neff and .ntff files individually. See Step 5: Upload your profile for the UI and command-line instructions.

For this first analysis, you profile RMSNorm, a small operation with a clear sequence of arithmetic and reduction operations.

You profile three implementations of the same operation:.

The scripts use the same inputs, profiler configuration, and schedule so the results are directly comparable.

All scripts to reproduce this work are available in the torch-neuronx examples directory.

Recent findings suggest that start by writing RMSNorm with individual PyTorch operations. Each line maps to one or more ATen operations and can create intermediate tensors.

Call the profiler with two arguments required for the Neuron backend:.

The schedule uses wait=2, warmup=1, and active=1 across four prof.step() calls. This records one warm iteration without including initial setup overhead.

Industry observers note that call torch.neuron.synchronize() inside the profiler loop. Without this synchronization, the profiler can export before the device finishes and leave the Neuron time column empty.

Industry observers note that after profiling finishes, inspect the key_averages() table. Sort by self_privateuse1_time_total to place the operations with the highest device cost first. The table shown here is filtered to the RMSNorm operations that report Neuron device time. The full key_averages() output also includes CPU-side events such as allocations and host-to-device transfers.

The key averages table shows that three aten::mul calls account for the largest share of Neuron device time.

The table highlights which ATen operations ran, how often they ran, and how much time they spent on the CPU and Neuron device. aten::mul has the highest total device time because the function performs three multiplications.

Each row maps directly to the function. aten::mul runs for x * x, x * rms, and the final multiplication by weight. aten::mean reduces the last dimension. aten::add adds the epsilon value and triggers a host-to-device copy because the scalar starts on the CPU. aten::rsqrt computes the reciprocal square root.

Neuron Explorer follows an aten::mul operation from framework dispatch through runtime scheduling to execution on the Neuron hardware lanes.

Sources indicate that in Explorer, time flows from left to right and the event lifecycle flows from top to bottom. Each ATen operation follows the same pattern: creation in the framework lane, scheduling in the runtime lane as nrta_execute_schedule, and device execution in the hardware lane as nc_exec_running.

Recent findings suggest that the system trace view organizes events into lanes. In the Default grouping mode, labels follow the pattern instance/PID/subsystem/identifier:.

Sources indicate that in eager mode, each operation runs independently. Use the dependency chain viewer to follow aten::mul.Tensor from the framework layer through runtime scheduling to device execution.

The dependency chain viewer highlights the lifecycle of one operation across the framework, runtime, and hardware lanes.

Replace the individual operations with PyTorch's built-in rms_norm function. Neuron lowers the operation to one fused kernel:.

The fused RMSNorm appears as one device operation in the key averages table.

The fused RMSNorm follows one framework-to-hardware path instead of dispatching each arithmetic operation separately.

It has been revealed that in the naive implementation, each operation crosses the dispatch boundary independently and follows its own framework-to-runtime-to-hardware path. In the fused implementation, one Python call covers the complete computation. The trace contains one dispatch and one hardware event, with no gaps between component operations.

For the final example, compile the original naive RMSNorm function with torch.compile.

With @torch.compile(backend="neuron"), TorchDynamo captures the Python bytecode as an FX graph and AOTAutograd lowers it to ATen operations. The Neuron backend receives the complete graph instead of dispatching each operation separately. It fuses the operations, optimizes memory access, and compiles the graph into a single NEFF artifact. The artifact runs as one hardware dispatch.

The compiled function appears as one Torch-Compiled Region in the key averages table.

The compiled graph follows one path through runtime scheduling and hardware execution.

Recent findings suggest that the table reveals one device execution, as in Profile 2, but the code takes a different path. Instead of calling a purpose-built fused operation, the compiler discovers the fusion from the original Python function. In this run, the Neuron time is comparable to torch.rms_norm, at 375 μs compared with 403 μs.

Industry observers note that both torch.rms_norm and torch.compile fuse RMSNorm into one kernel dispatch. In these runs, either approach takes about one-sixth of the naive implementation's device time. Fusion removes the gaps between hardware executions and avoids materializing intermediate values such as x_sq and mean_sq between separately dispatched operations.

key_averages() shows which operations consume device time, while its full output also reveals CPU-side setup and transfers. Explorer provides the corresponding visual trace. You can follow one operation from framework dispatch through runtime scheduling to hardware execution and see the gaps that fusion removes.

You can use the same workflow on larger models: find a hotspot in the table, verify it in the trace, and then determine whether a fused operation or torch.compile can reduce its cost.

Industry observers note that in Part 2, we will move into the device-level profile. You open the NEFF, inspect the TensorEngine, VectorEngine, and direct memory access (DMA) breakdown, and place the kernel on the roofline to determine whether it is compute-bound or memory-bound.

  • Recent findings suggest that the approach starts with material a filmmaker has already shot.

📑 Quick Jump: 1. Overview • 2. Key Details • 3. Closing Notes

Recent findings suggest that topview is expanding its hybrid filmmaking toolset with AI post-production controls for relighting, selective edits, newly introduced camera angles, background replacement, and other changes to live-action footage. Video Relight, the lighting component of the suite, is launching November 19.

Recent findings suggest that the approach starts with material a filmmaker has already shot. Rather than generating every scene from scratch, Topview aims to help editors repair or extend an existing take while preserving its surrounding composition and visual continuity.

That is a different production challenge from creating an isolated AI clip. A successful edit has to fit the actor’s performance, the camera movement, and the shots around it. The value of these tools depends on how much control they give filmmakers over the specific element they want to change.

Industry observers note that video Relight uses a 3D lighting interface to let creators adjust the number of lights and each light’s angle, color temperature, distance, softness, and intensity. A real-time plaster-sphere preview demonstrates the lighting setup before the creator generates a result.

Those controls make the intended effect more explicit than a prompt such as “make this scene warmer.” Color temperature changes the apparent warmth or coolness of the light; softness affects the transition between light and shadow; and position changes how illumination falls across the subject.

The sphere preview is a guide to the lighting arrangement, rather than a claim that the full video is regenerated in real time. The final shot still needs to carry that arrangement consistently through movement and changing views of the subject.

Topview also lists a Change Time & Weather tool for altering the time of day, weather, and moon phase. Its intended uses range from matching footage captured under different outdoor conditions to creating an environment that could not easily be filmed on location.

It has been revealed that video Element Edit offers several ways to specify a target: a text prompt, a selection box, a click, or a brush selection. The company says the tool is designed to adjust the selected area without affecting the rest of the shot.

According to recent reports, topview’s existing video-editing workflow also emphasizes selecting the moment that needs attention and guiding the change with natural-language instructions or a reference image. The new toolset extends that emphasis on targeted intervention into more filmmaking tasks.

Layer Edit addresses a related problem from another direction. It separates a video into elements that creators can move, resize, redraw, or edit. That could help an editor adjust composition or remove clutter without treating the entire frame as one inseparable image.

The practical distinction is control over both location and duration. Selecting an object in one frame is only the beginning; the change must remain attached to the right element as the actor or camera moves. For filmmakers, a clean still frame is useful only if the result also holds together in motion.

It has been revealed that camera Angle Presets generate additional views from existing live-action footage. Topview positions this as a way to fill a missing shot when returning to the set is impractical.

A synthesized angle is a newly introduced interpretation of the scene, so editors need to judge it against the source take: character appearance, positions, props, lighting, and the direction of movement all contribute to whether it cuts convincingly with the surrounding footage.

Add Extras lets creators place AI background performers into a scene and control where they stand and what they do. Topview says the tool is designed to produce varied crowds rather than obvious repetitions.

Industry observers note that the background tools cover two production situations. Replace Green Screen is intended to automate compositing, including difficult boundaries such as hair, translucent materials, and green spill. Replace Background works without a green screen, allowing selected parts of a location to be replaced or extended.

For a period scene, that might mean removing a modern building from an outdoor shot. For a production filmed in a confined space, it could mean extending the apparent setting. In each case, matching the subject’s lighting and the scene’s perspective determines whether the replacement feels integrated.

In a recent development, topview’s website describes an agent-based production platform that can plan scenes, choose models, generate assets, and keep shots editable in its Canvas workspace. Its broader offering spans short films, marketing videos, and microdramas, with model and asset management in the same environment.

The hybrid filmmaking tools add another route through that platform: footage captured with real actors becomes the starting material, and AI is used for particular post-production decisions.

The tech giant is led by co-founder and CEO Jensen Wu and co-founder and CTO Albert Chen. According to the supplied founder biographies, both worked on Taobao’s short-video platform, bringing product and engineering experience in video to Topview’s filmmaking ambitions.

Three additional capabilities are listed as coming soon. Adjust Eye Direction would use a visual 3D head model to change a performer’s gaze. Adjust Micro-Expressions would provide a 3D facial interface for controlling expressions. Amplify Performance would heighten expressions and body language when converting live action into an anime style.

Sources indicate that these are distinct from the November 19 Video Relight launch. They also reach further into the performance itself, where small changes can alter the meaning or emotional rhythm of a scene.

Industry observers note that for filmmakers, the immediate proposition is greater control over footage they already have: changing light, repairing a local detail, extending a setting, or exploring another view. Whether that saves a shot depends on the output staying consistent enough to survive the edit alongside the original material.

#46342. Latest Update: How Specializing the Vocabulary of SLMs Can Cut Inference Cost by 77% in Real Applications

📅 21 Oct 2026 • ⏱️ 11m • 📚 Deep Dive (2206 w)
📖 Baca

Latest Update: How Specializing the Vocabulary of SLMs Can Cut Inference Cost by 77% in Real Applications

📅 21 Oct 2026 | ⏱️ 11 min read (2206 words, 📚 Deep Dive) | Source: Hugging Face

⏱️ ~11 mins left to finish
📖 0% read
💡 Key Takeaways
  • Models specialized for a domain or a task by fine-tuning general open-source models, such as Qwen and Gemma, inherit a vocabulary built for many domains and general applications.
  • According to recent reports, in an essay grader we run in production, that vocabulary split the text the model writes most into many tokens.
  • In a recent development, the tokenizer is usually treated as a fixed property of the base model, inherited and left alone.
📑 Quick Jump: 1. Overview • 2. Key Details • 3. Closing Notes

Models specialized for a domain or a task by fine-tuning general open-source models, such as Qwen and Gemma, inherit a vocabulary built for many domains and general applications.

According to recent reports, in an essay grader we run in production, that vocabulary split the text the model writes most into many tokens. This article previews some results from the VocabX paper, which we will publish soon: how we specialized the vocabulary around the cost of each token rather than its frequency, and cut measured inference cost by 77% without changing the base model.

In a recent development, the tokenizer is usually treated as a fixed property of the base model, inherited and left alone. For a model specialized in a single domain, it can be one of the largest cost levers, and it is set before any training step.

According to recent reports, one of the systems we run in production is an automated grader for Portuguese essays, built on Qwen3-4B. It receives the essay, the prompt and the supporting texts, and returns a JSON assessment with a grade and a comment for each competency.

The model was already small, at 4 billion parameters, and had already been trained for the task. Its tokenizer, however, was still the original Qwen3-4B one, built for many languages and many kinds of text. In the grader, it was used for a single language, Portuguese, and a single response format. That had two costs: the text the grader writes on every request took more tokens than it needed, and at every generated token the model scored a vocabulary of 151,669 entries, including many this task almost never uses.

We rebuilt that vocabulary with a method we call VocabX, keeping the same base model, the same data and the same training recipe. The numbers in this article come from the current version of the paper, still under review, and may change before publication.

The leading language models read and write in tokens, and the tokenizer decides how text becomes tokens. The tokenizers of the leading general-purpose models are trained on large collections of text from many domains and languages, from source code to contracts to Chinese. For a general-purpose model, that choice makes sense.

For a model used in a single domain, it creates two kinds of waste at once.

The first is fragmentation. The tokenizer splits into many pieces exactly what the domain repeats most. In the grader, every response starts with the same JSON envelope, the same competency names, the same evaluation phrases. In contracts, it is the boilerplate clauses. In code, the identifiers. Each of these sequences costs several tokens where one would do, and the model pays for every one of them on every request.

The second is excess. The vocabulary carries tens of thousands of entries the domain never uses, and the model computes a score for all of them at every token it generates. A model tuned to grade American school biology exams will almost never write in Chinese, yet it computes the probability of every Chinese-language token at every step. The vocabulary splits into many pieces what the domain repeats most, and carries entries the domain never uses.

According to recent reports, the natural reaction is to count tokens and try to reduce the count. But the count is not the bill.

To see why a generated token costs more, it helps to look at how inference works. It has two phases. In prefill, the model processes the whole input in a single pass through the network: each weight read from GPU memory is reused for every input token, and the limit is compute. In decode, the model generates the response one token at a time, and each token needs a full pass. Each weight read is used only a few times, and the GPU spends most of its time waiting for data to arrive from memory: the limit becomes memory bandwidth.

This effect is strongest exactly where we operate: small models served with moderate batches. Batching requests splits the weight reads across them and eases the problem, but does not solve it. At every decode step, the model also reads the KV cache, the attention memory that holds the context already processed and grows with it. In the case we measured, the grader, a generated token costs 7.4 times a token read, but the ratio varies with the hardware, the problem, the batch size, the context length and other factors, and it can be larger than that. In general, the direction holds: generating costs more than reading.

In a recent development, think of a shipping tech giant that charges per box, but charges seven times more for outgoing boxes than for incoming ones. Reducing the total number of boxes helps. Reducing the outgoing boxes helps seven times more. A method that compresses input and output equally misses most of the possible savings.

It has been revealed that the third component of the bill is the vocabulary itself. The model's last layer, the LM head, turns the internal state into a score for every possible token. To do that, it holds one row of parameters per vocabulary entry. In a model the size of Qwen3-4B, that matrix accounts for almost 10% of the parameters. It is a share that large models absorb without noticing, but it weighs on a small model.

In a recent development, and the cost is not paid only once. The input layer looks up only the row of the token being read, but the LM head reads and multiplies the entire matrix for every generated token. Since decode is already memory-bound, every extra row is more data to move at every step. An entry the domain never uses costs exactly the same as a frequent one. That is why adding tokens can lower the count and raise the bill at the same time. VocabX does not include this term in its selection criterion, but it controls vocabulary size in two steps: the sub-word merge replaces the base vocabulary with a smaller, domain-specific one, and macros enter under a fixed budget. In the grader, the output layer went from about 152,000 to about 65,000 rows.

Industry observers note that adapting a model's vocabulary is not a upcoming idea. Reference methods in the literature, such as fast vocabulary transfer (FVT), multi-word tokenization (MWT) and Liquid AI's in-place tokenizer expansion (in-place BPE), which continues BPE training from the original vocabulary, already reduce fragmentation. When we tested them on our problem, we found two limitations.

They choose tokens by frequency, not by cost. An expression that appears often in the input is worth more to them than one that appears less often in the response, even if the second is the more expensive one to serve.

They work on a single layer. They either adjust how words are cut into pieces, or merge whole phrases into one token. None of these three does both under the same criterion. And the grader's biggest waste was precisely in long, repeated spans such as the JSON envelope, which a sub-word method only reaches after merging each part, one by one.

VocabX addresses both limitations, plus a third problem that appears on the obvious path to solving the first.

First, we changed the question. Instead of asking how many tokens a candidate saves, we ask how much cost and time it saves. Each eliminated token is multiplied by the price of the field it appears in: system prompt, user message or model response. In the case we measured, the grader, a token saved in the response is worth 7.4 times one saved in the input, and the vocabulary is built accordingly.

Industry observers note that second, we work on both layers at once. Back to the shipping tech giant: you can cut boxes by packing each item better, or by recognizing that the same twelve-item kit ships every week and sending the kit in a single box. VocabX does both. At the sub-word layer, it rebuilds how domain words are cut into pieces. At the multi-word layer, it looks for whole spans that repeat, from short expressions to full lines and JSON envelopes, and turns each into a single token, which we call a macro token. Both layers are chosen under the same cost criterion, each with its own budget.

To find these spans, we use five miners, automatic searches for spans that repeat across the corpus, each specialized in one kind of repetition: long words, whole lines, expressions, complete sentences, and structures with punctuation such as JSON and tags. Averaged over eight corpora, the last one contributed the most, and on code it alone accounted for 17.5 points. Without all five, token reduction on the grader would drop by 55.6 points.

Recent findings suggest that third, we estimate what the sample cannot see. Choosing tokens by cost requires knowing how much each candidate still saves after the ones already chosen. Measuring that exactly would require reprocessing the entire corpus after every choice, tens of thousands of times. A common way to do this at scale is to measure on a sample of documents, and then a candidate absent from the sample gets zero gain.

Recent findings suggest that an expression that appears 37 times in 50,000 documents demonstrates up in a 400-document sample only about 26% of the time. In a contracts corpus, only 16.6% of the candidates appear in a 400-document sample; the rest are never evaluated.

Industry observers note that A candidate's gain has two parts. One is how much it saves over the entire corpus, and that can be counted exactly, without a sample. The other is how much of that saving is not yet covered by the tokens already chosen, and only that part needs to be estimated. For candidates the sample cannot see, we use a statistical estimate based on the behavior of the ones it can see, instead of zero. A candidate that is rare in the sample but frequent in the corpus is back in the running.

That change alone, with the same sample and the same budget, raised token reduction on a contracts corpus from 44.7% to 52.8%.

To measure the real effect, we trained seven versions of the grader with the same base model, the same data, the same recipe and the same seed. The only difference between them is the tokenizer. All of them ran the same 500 requests on the same test machine, with an RTX 5090 GPU and the vLLM inference server, and cost was calculated from measured runtime.

The model's response dropped from 350 to 101 tokens on average. Cost dropped 77.0%. Quality, measured by the bench score, which combines grading accuracy and the accuracy of screening off-topic or rule-breaking essays, rose from 0.703 to 0.810.

Industry observers note that getting there required a course correction. The first version of the vocabulary fused each competency's grade with the surrounding JSON into a single macro token. It was the most compact option, but quality dropped: its bench score was 0.689, below the production grader's 0.703. With the grade inside the macro, each combination of grade and structure became a different variant of the same token, and the model chose both in a single step. Giving the grade its own token cost 2 extra tokens per response, raised the bench score to 0.810 and, in the measurement, was even cheaper: a 77.0% reduction, against 73.3% for the fused version.

The lesson applies beyond the grader. Compression has a cost when the compressed span carries the very decision the model exists to make. The goal is not the cheapest possible vocabulary, but the cheapest one that preserves the tokens that matter.

Recent findings suggest that to find out whether the gain was specific to our case, we compared VocabX with the three reference methods on five public domains (contracts, medical papers, scientific papers, news and Python code) and three model families (Qwen3, Llama-3.1 and Gemma-3). All methods used the same mining and test documents, and the same vocabulary ceiling.

VocabX compressed more than the strongest reference method in all fifteen combinations, by 1.2 to 9.3 points. In estimated inference cost, the pruned version of VocabX also led in all fifteen, with average margins of 10.2 points on Qwen3, 7.5 on Llama-3.1 and 13.6 on Gemma-3. On contracts, the pruned version reached 62.6% token reduction with 113,426 vocabulary entries, against 61.8% for the best in-place BPE configuration, which uses 207,803.

Industry observers note that vocabX does not make the model smarter. It makes the model stop paying for text it does not need to write piece by piece, and stop scoring a vocabulary it will never use. In our grader, that cut measured inference cost by 77%, with the same base model and the same training recipe.

Specialization usually starts with data and weights. It can also start one layer earlier, in the vocabulary.

The full method, the tables for every experiment and the discarded interventions will be in the VocabX paper, which we will publish soon.

📅 19 Nov 2026 | ⏱️ 4 min read (797 words, 📚 Deep Dive) | Source: Infoq

⏱️ ~4 mins left to finish
📖 0% read
💡 Key Takeaways
  • InfoQ Homepage News .NET 11 : ASP.NET Core: Union Type Support, OpenAPI 3.2 by Default and Blazor AI Components.
  • Nov 19, 2026 3 min read.
  • Last week, Microsoft shipped ASP.NET Core in .NET 11 as part of the wider .NET 11 release.
📑 Quick Jump: 1. Overview • 2. Key Details • 3. Closing Notes

InfoQ Homepage News .NET 11 : ASP.NET Core: Union Type Support, OpenAPI 3.2 by Default and Blazor AI Components.

Nov 19, 2026 3 min read.

Last week, Microsoft shipped ASP.NET Core in .NET 11 as part of the wider .NET 11 release. The update spans Minimal APIs, OpenAPI, SignalR, Blazor, authentication, and the Kestrel server. As stated in the announcement, .NET 11 is a Standard Term Support release with two years of support.

Industry observers note that on the API side, developers can now use C# 15 union types in JSON request and response bodies across Minimal APIs and MVC. The release notes limit the feature to JSON bodies, so route, query, header, and form values cannot bind to a union.

Minimal API validation also runs asynchronous validators, which keeps threads free while a rule waits on a database lookup or a remote call. The framework can now localize validation messages and display names itself, and endpoints can skip the remaining middleware pipeline through a newly introduced [ShortCircuit] attribute.

Developers who generate OpenAPI documents now get version 3.2 unless they select an earlier one for tooling that has not caught up. As described in the release notes, the framework depends on Microsoft.OpenApi 3.3.1 for this, and the notes label that update a breaking change.

Recent findings suggest that with 3.2, endpoints that stream server-sent events are documented with a schema for each event's payload, and the generator emits an anyOf schema for unions. Generated documents can also describe endpoints that use the HTTP QUERY method, and APIs that carry the [Obsolete] attribute show up as deprecated.

SignalR adds authentication refresh, so a long-lived connection no longer has to close when its access token expires. As reported, server developers enable it per hub, while the .NET client refreshes automatically by default and the TypeScript client can do the same. Blazor passes the refreshed identity on to Interactive Server components while the circuit stays connected.

Sources indicate that blazor receives the longest list of changes, and many of them target static server-side rendering. With the fresh CacheView component, developers can cache the rendered markup of a component subtree, and the child components do not run when a cached copy is served. Blazor now ships client-side validation for static SSR forms, enabled by default.

Developers can also carry data between requests with TempData or session values. According to the release notes, the Blazor Web App template drops its app.UseAntiforgery() call, because a middleware for CSRF protection is now added by default.

For Interactive Server apps, an opt-in package pauses the circuit of a hidden browser tab after a delay, two minutes by default, to free server memory. Lists built with Virtualize may now mix items of different heights, and Microsoft raised the default OverscanCount from 3 to 15. Page and sort state in QuickGrid now lives in the URL query string, with sortable headers and pager controls rendered as links instead of buttons.

Industry observers note that the release notes flag this as a CSS breaking change, because custom styles written for the buttons also have to target the links. The release also includes Microsoft.AspNetCore.Components.AI, a set of components for chat and agent interfaces. According to the announcement, Microsoft treats that package as experimental and will keep it in prerelease throughout .NET 11.

On the security and server side, an experimental package adds Device Bound Session Credentials, a protocol that ties session refresh to a private key held by the browser. Response compression and request decompression gain Zstandard support, which is on by default.

Kestrel's HTTP/1.1 parser no longer throws exceptions on malformed requests, a change that is reported to raise throughput by up to 20 to 40 percent under heavy invalid traffic. The shared framework libraries of ASP.NET Core are now compiled with runtime-async, described in the release notes as an internal change with no public API impact.

Two older APIs are on the way out. The Microsoft.AspNetCore.Grpc.Swagger package is now deprecated, and Kestrel's TlsClientHelloBytesCallback option is obsolete in favor of the new UseTlsClientHelloListener extension.

Other changes in this release are native OpenTelemetry tracing attributes, client-side cancellation of SignalR hub invocations, scrolling to a specific item in Virtualize and QuickGrid, passkey display names inferred from the authenticator, and TimeProvider support in ASP.NET Core Identity.

For interested readers and developers, the full release notes are available in the What's upcoming in ASP.NET Core in .NET 11 article on Microsoft Learn.

📑 Quick Jump: 1. Overview • 2. Key Details • 3. Closing Notes

Sources indicate that google declared on November 19, 2026 that Blue Origin’s Upcoming Glenn will conduct Project Suncatcher’s first dedicated heavy-lift launch, targeted for the first quarter of 2029. The companies’ launch services agreement covers deployment of solar-powered satellites carrying Google’s Tensor Processing Units, or TPUs, into sun-synchronous orbit.

Each satellite is designed to provide computing capacity roughly at the scale of a data center rack. The mission is part of Google’s research into whether an interconnected network of solar-powered satellites could scale machine-learning compute in space. The dedicated launch also builds on Google’s continuing work with other satellite and launch partners.

In a recent development, blue Origin’s Newly introduced Glenn specifications give the vehicle general lift ratings of 45 metric tons to low Earth orbit and more than 13 metric tons to geostationary transfer orbit. The seven-meter payload fairing provides twice the volume of smaller five-meter-class fairings, while the reusable first stage is designed for a minimum of 25 flights.

Jordan Charles, senior vice president of New Glenn at Blue Origin, said the rocket’s “heavy-lift capacity and large payload volume give customers the flexibility to bring new capabilities to orbit.” For Suncatcher, that combination is intended to serve a multi-satellite deployment, moving beyond the single-prototype stage of the research.

The agreement follows Google’s September 2026 Project Suncatcher prototype preview and its subsequent in-orbit TPU response. A prototype satellite launched on October 1, 2026; by October 30, 2026, Google had powered the host and TPU trays and run early machine-learning tests during commissioning. Its onboard Gemma 4 model generated a haiku, which Google described as the first AI response from a data-center-class TPU in orbit. The disclosed plan continues with thermal-stress and radiation testing, followed by a planned 2027 milestone of two interconnected satellites.

Google indicates satellites in low Earth orbit can access near-constant sunlight and generate up to eight times more solar power than on Earth, forming Project Suncatcher’s energy rationale. Proposed future designs place dozens of TPUs on each satellite and use lasers for high-bandwidth communication over short distances between spacecraft orbiting in clusters.

Beyond power generation, the proposed cluster poses cooling and communications problems. In a vacuum, chips cannot rely on airflow; engineers have tested heat pipes and radiators in a thermal vacuum chamber. The laser links must maintain high bandwidth over short distances between moving spacecraft, requiring precise knowledge of each satellite’s position relative to its neighbors.

Sources indicate that the agreement supplies a heavy-lift path for a larger research deployment, while the prototype and twin-satellite work must still establish the essentials of orbital computing: reliable chips, effective cooling and precise intersatellite communication. That sequence makes the upcoming tests central to whether Suncatcher can progress from individual machines running in orbit to a networked machine-learning system.

Her work explores how AI systems are accelerating discovery beyond Earth—from satellite imaging and autonomous navigation to deep-space research and planetary science.

With a visionary yet scientifically rigorous perspective, Lyra bridges hard data with cosmic curiosity, examining how machine learning supports astronomical observation, mission planning, and the interpretation of vast streams of space data. She is particularly interested in how AI expands humanity’s ability to observe, map, and understand the universe at scales previously beyond reach.

Turning Database Grading into RL Rewards: Post-Training Agents with ThinkingBox

📅 22 Oct 2026 | ⏱️ 16 min read (3166 words, 📚 Deep Dive) | Source: Hugging Face

⏱️ ~16 mins left to finish
📖 0% read
💡 Key Takeaways
  • It has been revealed that this is the follow up to our first blog post, The Agent Noted It Was Done.
  • Recent findings suggest that we built ThinkingBox to evaluate an agent's work by comparing the final database state with the expected outcome.
  • ThinkingBox turns executable checks of terminal database state into rewards for post-training agents on tasks outside ThinkingBox-Bench.
📑 Quick Jump: 1. Overview • 2. Key Details • 3. Closing Notes

It has been revealed that this is the follow up to our first blog post, The Agent Noted It Was Done. The Database Disagreed. ThinkingBox-Training is now available on GitHub.

Recent findings suggest that we built ThinkingBox to evaluate an agent's work by comparing the final database state with the expected outcome. We then used the same kind of executable signal as a reward on training tasks outside ThinkingBox-Bench. For Qwen3.8-27B, average success rose from 51.70% to 60.78%, while tasks completed correctly on all twenty attempts rose from 38 to 107 with 50 GRPO steps.

Figure 1. ThinkingBox turns executable checks of terminal database state into rewards for post-training agents on tasks outside ThinkingBox-Bench.

We built ThinkingBox to catch agents that say they are done when they are not.

Each of its 507 tasks in ThinkingBox-Bench (our benchmark dataset) hands an agent a real backend and a set of tools, lets it work, then checks what really changed in the database. In the first post, we caught a model closing a customer's ticket as resolved while the carrier exception behind it was still open. Nine competent-looking tool calls, one wrong database row.

Then we noticed what we had built. For most tasks, an executable check can return 1 or 0 directly from the final database state. That is not just a grader. This can be a reward function.+.

It has been revealed that so we constructed a training pool from ThinkingBox-format tasks outside the benchmark and used their executable outcomes as rewards. The catch was choosing which tasks are suitable for agent training: most tasks are either already solved or hopeless for the model in front of you, and both teach it nothing.

Difficulty is policy-relative: a task is hard for the current model only until that model learns it.

We call this offline policy-relative difficulty. We estimated each task's success probability once using the base policy before training and kept the selected training pool fixed throughout the run.

We used offline policy-relative difficulty to build the training pool, then fine-tuned Qwen3.8-27B with GRPO for 50 steps. To recap, we evaluate each of the 507 benchmark tasks 20 times. pass@1 measures average success across all 10,140 attempts. pass@20 measures the share of tasks solved at least once. Observed 20/20 measures the share of tasks that pass every recorded attempt.

Table 1. Qwen3.8-27B results before and after 50 steps of GRPO on the offline-selected training pool.

Sources indicate that training sharply increased repeatable success, with a small decline in at-least-once coverage. The rest of the post explains how we selected practice tasks, built the reward loop, and measured that tradeoff.

According to recent reports, what does that improvement look like on one task? A traveler requests a room downgrade, but firm policy requires manager approval first. Before training, the agent changed the booking and issued refunds without approval in 15 of 20 attempts. After RL fine-tuning, it preserved the booking and payment state in all 20.

According to recent reports, figure 2. One corporate hotel-booking task, 20 attempts per model. The base Qwen3.8-27B model changed the booking without required manager approval in 15 attempts. The RL fine-tuned model preserved booking and payment state in all 20; all expected records matched in 19.

In a hurry? The headline result is above. The implementation is in Run the training stack.

ThinkingBox-Bench grades agents on the database records they leave behind. Each of its 507 tasks starts a real backend, hands the agent a set of MCP tools and a simulated LLM user with private context, and at the end runs executable checks against the terminal database state. Checks are against the backend record that needs to be correct, not the specific tool calls. This incentivizes the model to discover possibly upcoming solution paths rather than “rediscover” the human-backed solution, that might be suboptimal albeit correct.

It has been revealed that in our first post we ran eighteen models through that benchmark twenty times each and reported a gap that headline accuracy hides. Kimi-K3 solved 93.89% of tasks at least once but completed only 68 of 507 tasks (13.41%) on all twenty recorded attempts. Claude Opus 5 inverted it: narrower coverage, far more consistency.

And bigger or better model did not close it. Claude Opus 5.5 scored 0.66 percentage points higher than Claude Opus 5 on pass@1, yet passed exactly the same number of tasks, 241, on all twenty attempts. That gain in headline accuracy bought zero additional dependability.

In a recent development, if you are choosing a model for work that touches production database records, pass@1 should not be read alone. Observed 20/20 shows which tasks succeed on every attempt, which is closer to what production reliability requires.

Recent findings suggest that the executable terminal-state verdict was also the training reward. Before unpacking the training loop, here is what changed on the sealed benchmark.

Sources indicate that after training Qwen3.8-27B, we evaluated the selected step-50 checkpoint on the 507-task benchmark it had never trained on. The 507 tasks represent an out-of-distribution test set: their domains, databases, and most MCP tools were not encountered during RL training.

It has been revealed that table 2. ThinkingBox-Bench pass@1 (%) by domain, for selected models from our first blog's Table 2 and our fine-tuned model for different domains and overall. Observed 20/20 numbers are over the entire benchmark with 507 tasks. Each model is evaluated on all 507 tasks for 20 repeated trials. Bold marks the column leader; underline marks the runner-up.

Sources indicate that the headline result is the observed-20/20 row in Table 1. A 27B model that initially completed 38 (7.5%) of ThinkingBox-Bench on every attempt now completes 107 (21.1%) on every attempt, almost thrice. For comparison, observed 20/20 for Kimi-K3 is 68, GPT-5.4 with 128, GPT-6 Astra has 231, and Claude Opus 5.5 leads with 241.

Industry observers note that average success and repeatability produce different orderings. In Table 2, we notice that GPT-5.6 Sol scored slightly higher on pass@1 than the RL fine-tuned Qwen3.8-27B (61.91% versus 60.78%) but passed fewer tasks on all 20 recorded attempts: 82 versus 107. Claude Sonnet 4.6 scored lower on pass@1, at 59.19%, yet passed nearly the same number of tasks every time, at 102. Neither metric alone captures the full picture.

The observed pattern is consistent with sharpening: repeatable success rose while at-least-once coverage fell slightly. This is in-line with prior work. One explanation is that probability distribution moved toward trajectories that work repeatedly while some low-probability paths disappeared.

Recent findings suggest that overall, the model did not become broader. It became more repeatable. The next question is where those gains landed.

Figure 3. Domain-level base scores, RLFT scores, and percentage-point changes. Green change cells show gains and red cells show declines; blue shading indicates the score level within each metric.

In a recent development, pass@1 and observed 20/20 rose in all five domains. Pass@20 was mixed: it increased in neobank and consulting, but declined in retail, travel, and auto insurance. Auto insurance had the largest breadth loss (−7.0 points), while retail had the largest observed-20/20 gain (+24.5 points).

The first post priced consistency using simple math: divide the estimated cost of the full 20-run campaign by the number of tasks the model passed every single time.

Cost per dependable task = estimated cost of the 507 × 20 campaign ÷ tasks passing 20/20.

Applying the same cost math to the fine-tuned checkpoint's measured token usage:.

Table 3. Estimated evaluation cost and dependability for base and RL fine-tuned Qwen3.8-27B. Cost per successful attempt divides total estimated campaign cost (507 x 20) by the number of passing attempts.

At $8.00 per dependable task, the fine-tuned model came close to GPT-5.4 ($6.80), GPT-6 Astra ($7.45), and Claude Opus 5.5 ($7.80) in the companion comparison.

Figure 4 prices cost per successful attempt against pass@1.

Sources indicate that figure 4. The golden arrow traces Qwen3.8-27B base pareto cost position to the RLFT (diamond): pass@1 rises from 51.70% to 60.78% while estimated cost per successful attempt falls from $0.177 to $0.139. Ringed circles mark the Pareto cost frontier.

The move places the fine-tuned checkpoint close to GPT-5.6 Sol, although GPT-5.6 Sol remains cheaper and slightly higher on pass@1. Four models priced in our paper fall outside the plotted range.

According to recent reports, the dollar values are a comparative serving index, not invoice or cloud bills. Serving the fine-tuned checkpoint would be the same as the base model. The calculation includes model inference cost, and excludes training run and policy-probe cost for curating the training dataset.

Recent findings suggest that these results tell us what moved. The next sections explain the training loop and why selecting the right tasks matters the most.

Figure 5. The six stages, now in context: candidate tasks feed in, the first three run once offline, the last three repeat for every group in the training run. The trained checkpoint is evaluated against ThinkingBox-Bench.

Recent findings suggest that selection runs once, offline, against the base policy model, i.e in this case Qwen3.8 27B; training then uses that fixed pool that has been curated. The dashed amber arrow in Figure 5 marks the path we did not take: re-probing difficulty during the training run.

Every rollout is a complete episode, not a text completion. It gets a fresh backend, an isolated MCP session, and GPT-5 Chat as the simulated user. Most rewards come from deterministic terminal-state checks; a minority of narrow rubric requirements can invoke the configured judge (GPT-5 Chat).

Training and evaluation must interpret Qwen output identically. That includes reasoning extraction, tool calls, argument typing, rendering, and isolated task state. Otherwise the reward measures a different agent from the one evaluated. The shared interpretation code is in trainer/core/tb_interpret.py.

For the reference run, we ran full-parameter RL fine-tuned Qwen3.8-27B on 187 tasks using token-mean GRPO. Each update generated 18 groups of 8 rollouts, or 144 episodes, across 24 H100s. Training ran synchronously with parameter and optimizer offload; AdamW used a 1e-6 learning rate and zero weight decay. We ran the training for 50 steps.

Recent findings suggest that zero-variance groups were replaced DAPO-style during training. System errors were handled separately: a backend timeout is not an incorrect agent outcome, so affected groups were refilled rather than scored as failures.

That explains how retained tasks were trained. The remaining question is which tasks entered the training pool.

Before diving deep into the selection of training tasks, a disclaimer:.

Sources indicate that no ThinkingBox-Bench task was included in the RL training pool. The benchmark was reserved for evaluation.

According to recent reports, thinkingBox-Bench is out-of-distribution relative to the RL training pool: its domains, databases, policies, and most tools were not encountered during RL training. The two sets still share the ThinkingBox framework, simulated-user machinery, executable terminal-state grading, a few common tools, and a similar task style. These shared elements limit the scope of the transfer claim.

Sources indicate that why selection matters comes down to one arithmetic fact about GRPO. If all eight rollouts fail, the reward vector is [0, 0, 0, 0, 0, 0, 0, 0]. If all eight succeed, it is [1, 1, 1, 1, 1, 1, 1, 1]. In either case, centering within the group produces no task-reward advantage because no trajectory did better than another.++.

A mixed group such as [0, 0, 0, 1, 1, 1, 1, 1] supplies the contrast GRPO can learn from. That distinction is expensive for a stateful agent: every rollout provisions an isolated backend, runs a real tool session, and calls a separate model to play the user.

Recent findings suggest that the question that shaped this work was therefore not only which model or optimizer? It was: which candidate tasks should enter the fixed training pool?

We used an offline pass-rate filter on the posterior to select the training pool. It estimates which tasks are likely to produce contrasting terminal rewards under the base policy.

According to recent reports, so we probe. Each candidate task is run repeatedly against the base policy model. The plain-language rule is simple: tasks the model always fails are unlikely to teach it yet; tasks it always passes are already learned; tasks it solves sometimes are where outcomes can provide contrast.

Industry observers note that each candidate task is run n times, producing k successes. We model its latent success probability with Jeffreys posterior probability:.

success probability | k successes in n probes ~ Beta(k + ½, n − k + ½).

According to recent reports, figure 6. Offline policy-relative difficulty is estimated from repeated base-policy probes and used to retain tasks likely to produce contrasting rewards.

We partition the unit interval into five buckets with boundaries at 0.08, 0.40, 0.60, and 0.90, chosen as hyperparameters for these runs. Each task is assigned to the bucket containing the greatest posterior mass:.

Further details are in Appendix C.4 of our ThinkingBox paper.

It has been revealed that figure 7. Zooming in, one task through all six stages: GPT-5.4 screening, base-model probes, difficulty classification, a rollout group, terminal-state grading, and a GRPO patch.

Figure 7 follows one candidate task that can potentially enter the training pool. For the Qwen3.8 27B full-parameter pool, GPT-5.4 first served as a solvability screen. The base policy then succeeded on few of the probes e.g 3 of 8, producing a Beta(3.5, 5.5) posterior. Its largest mass, 54.0%, fell in the Difficult band.

Recent findings suggest that when sampled for training, the task produced the mixed reward group [0, 0, 0, 0, 1, 1, 1, 1]. Successful trajectories therefore received above-mean task advantage and failed trajectories below-mean advantage, giving GRPO contrast to learn from. A different policy model could place the same task in a different difficulty band.

The final Qwen3.8-27B curated training pool contained 187 tasks.

According to recent reports, nothing about the trajectory. The reward is the task's own executable verdict.

According to recent reports, when an episode ends, the sandbox extracts what actually changed in the backend and runs the task's deterministic checks against the terminal state. Any trajectory that produces the correct end state passes. Wrong, missing, or extra side effects fail. The reward is 1 or 0.

Recent findings suggest that in the benchmark, the database grader can be thought of as the “examiner”: it caught agents that reported success and left the wrong record. In training, the same kind of check can be seen as the “teacher” on a different, disjoint set of tasks.

Two reward paths, one binary verdict.

It has been revealed that salesforce on November 19, 2026 detailed the cloud, data, AI model, security and application components of its designated Super Intelligence (SI) export package, after the U.S. Department of Commerce selected its consortium as one of 33 initial pre-set consortia in the American SI Exports Program.

Recent findings suggest that commerce announced the initial designations on November 16, 2026. Salesforce’s subsequent disclosure explains how its cloud, data and agent software fit that federally supported export structure, with sovereignty and deployment controls presented as central parts of the offer.

The offer draws on an established public-sector footprint. Salesforce notes its technology supports government operations in more than 30 countries, including work with 60 U.S. federal agencies, all 15 U.S. Cabinet departments and all 50 states. That experience connects the export package to an existing government business rather than treating it as a standalone model release.

At the infrastructure layer, Hyperforce, Salesforce’s cloud architecture, runs on leading U.S. cloud infrastructure that the company indicates supports local sovereignty and data-residency requirements. Data 360 and Zero Copy partners are designed to provide governed data without duplicating it across systems, while Informatica contributes data-governance and data-quality capabilities.

Sources indicate that at the model layer, the Atlas Reasoning Engine helps agents reason and act using Salesforce’s xGen models and third-party large language models, according to the company. Security controls come from the Einstein Trust Layer and Salesforce Shield, while Agentforce supplies pre-built agents for customer and constituent service, case management and operations. The package therefore combines model choice with the data and application layers needed to put agents into government workflows.

Kendall Collins, president and CEO of Missionforce and Government Cloud at Salesforce, stated the combination is intended to deliver faster public services and stronger operations “with model choice and controls that respect customers’ sovereignty.”.

The official program menu identifies Salesforce as the anchor member of the Salesforce Consortium, meaning it organizes and leads the group, assembles participating members and submits the proposal. U.S. and Foreign Commercial Service representatives and interagency partners will offer designated packages to foreign buyers globally, and U.S. government representatives can facilitate transactions with trusted buyers.

Pre-set consortia are standing teams that must cover the complete SI stack: SI-optimized hardware, data pipelines and labeling systems, models and systems, security and cybersecurity, and applications. Designation can bring priority government-to-government advocacy, priority consideration for transaction-specific export-control engagement, and priority routing for available federal financing referrals. The program’s rules condition that support on determinations of U.S. interest, applicable law and agency procedure, with financing referrals also subject to agency underwriting standards and program requirements.

The program implements Executive Order 14320, which directed Commerce to coordinate promotion of full-stack American SI technology exports. A second participation route opens for applications on November 30, 2026: on-demand consortia formed for an identified export opportunity need cover only the stack layers required by that deal. The program’s participation rules subject both routes to completeness and substantive reviews for national-interest designation.

The practical gain for Salesforce is distribution: a coordinated federal channel through which its cloud, data and agent portfolio can reach foreign buyers. Because the menu contains packages from many other technology providers, designation provides access to advocacy and deal facilitation rather than an exclusive position. The commercial test is whether federal advocacy and facilitation turn Salesforce’s menu listing into completed foreign deployments under the program’s transaction-specific requirements.

📑 Quick Jump: 1. Overview • 2. Key Details • 3. Closing Notes

In a recent development, in a previous post, we introduced TorchNeuron, the native PyTorch backend for AWS Trainium (the torch-neuronx package). With it, Transformers runs its own modeling code on Trainium, as it does on any other device, so any Transformers model on the Hub may run. Which ones actually do?

The torch-neuronx model support Space answers that question for the most popular models on the Hub. It tells you whether a model runs unmodified on Trainium, and gives you the script to run it yourself.

The Space opens on the Selected view: our own selection of models picked among the top models on the Hub by downloads and by trending score. Each row gives the result, the number of Trainium cores the model is sharded over, the wall time of the run (compilation included) and the peak device memory.

To look up a given model, switch to the Trending or Downloads view and type part of its name. These views follow the Hub's own rankings, one task at a time, whether a model was tested or not. When a model was left out on purpose, the Space tells you why (most of the time it was not prioritized, sometimes it is truly incompatible). You can also pick the versions of the Neuron compiler (neuronx-cc) and of Transformers to look at.

At the time of writing, only Transformers models are tested, and our selection is limited to text-generation and image-text-to-text models. We plan to expand to diffusers, sentence transformers, and other transformers tasks.

Select a model to see how to run it. The Space lists the Neuron stack the model was tested on, the packages to install on top of it, and the run.py script that ran. The script follows the recipe of the TorchNeuron announcement: it loads the model with from_pretrained, sharded when it needs to be, then generates with a static cache and torch.compile(backend="neuron").

On a Trainium2 (trn2) instance with that stack, for example in the AWS Neuron Deep Learning Container, install the packages, then run:.

No need for torchrun: the script releases its own torch.distributed ranks when the model is sharded.

A first run starts by compiling the model's graphs. To skip that step, copy the graphs the same compiler built during the test, from the public NEFF cache bucket. The Space gives you the command, with the right compiler version:.

Each test loads the model on a trn2 instance, sharded over the smallest number of Trainium cores that can hold its weights. Most models are sharded with tensor parallelism. Mixture-of-experts models without a tensor-parallel strategy use expert parallelism only. The test then generates 32 tokens and checks them. On a single core, the tokens are compared with those of a CPU run of the same checkpoint. When the model is sharded, a small judge model checks that the text is fluent English.

Industry observers note that at the time of writing, only models that fit on 4 Trainium2 devices are tested, which means 16 cores at most. A PASS says nothing about throughput, or about longer generations.

Everything the Space shows comes from the public aws-neuron/torch-neuronx-model-support dataset, with one Parquet file per pair of neuronx-cc and library versions.

Each row holds a model's result, the error when it failed, the versions of the whole stack and the run.py that ran. You can query it directly:.

The dataset card gives the exact meaning of each result.

Next time you wonder whether a model runs on Trainium, look it up.
