📑 Quick Jump: 1. Overview • 2. Key Details • 3. Closing Notes

The United Kingdom has issued economic sanctions against Cryptomus, a chameleonic cryptocurrency platform that experts say serves as a major conduit for payments related to ransomware, narcotics, darknet markets, fraud and cybercrime services that are helping Russia circumvent existing financial restrictions.

Heleket’s support agent on Telegram claims, despite all evidence to the contrary, that it is not affiliated with Cryptomus. Image: Richard Sanders.

Industry observers note that on October 8, the U.K. issued sanctions (PDF) against Cryptomus — previously known as Certa Payments and Xeltox Enterprises — for processing payments that benefit the Russian government and its financial institutions. The sanctions freeze any Cryptomus assets at U.K. banks, and bar British companies from offering it any business, virtual or otherwise. Also targeted in these sanctions were the virtual payment platforms VexPay, TokenSpot, and the Tsunami Payments service.

As explained in our December 2024 investigation, “How Cryptocurrency Turns to Cash in Russian Banks,” Cryptomus has been a key payment processor for dozens of Russian cryptocurrency exchanges and websites hawking cybercrime services. The company has changed its name several times since emerging in 2022, most recently to “Heleket” last year after Canada levied a record CAD $176 million fine against the platform for anti-money laundering violations.

The blockchain data-crunching firm Chainalysis stated the U.K. sanctions target the broader infrastructure supporting Russia’s wartime economy.

“Cryptomus and Heleket have emerged as major payment hubs for illicit activity,” Chainalysis wrote in an October 8 blog post. “Together, these services received more illicit funds across tracked categories than the mixers in our dataset and the number of illicit counterparties surged to more than 900 in a single month in late 2025.”.

The Cryptomus support bot on Telegram, responding on Oct. 8 to an inquiry by saying the platform was suddenly unable to process transactions.

In April 2026, the blockchain analysis firm TRM Labs found Cryptomus had processed more than $7 billion in transactions since its inception in 2022, including transactions associated with child sexual abuse material vendors, terrorist financing networks, and human trafficking operations.

TRM noted that Cryptomus’s transaction volume cratered after the platform instituted latest “know your customer” or KYC rules, and that the cryptocurrency platform responded to the Canadian fines by launching Heleket as a parallel service that continued to offer no-KYC payment processing.

According to recent reports, richard Sanders is a blockchain analyst and investigator who spent months mapping out Cryptomus’s payment infrastructure and transacting with its customers. Sanders noted the U.K. sanctions on Cryptomus are important because Canada’s fine against the platform was ultimately unenforceable and uncollectible.

“A fine doesn’t stop a cryptocurrency payment processor from processing payments,” Sanders wrote on LinkedIn. “Sanctions kill the operation. The distinction matters.”.

Industry observers note that as our 2024 investigation noted, Cryptomus shared a Vancouver address with dozens of other foreign currency dealers and money transfer businesses — none of which appeared to be physically located there. Following the CAD $176 million fine for alleged money laundering violations, Cryptomus appealed the penalty, launched Heleket as a parallel service, and kept on processing large volumes of sketchy transactions, Sanders remarked.

Sanders noted the sanctions also are notable because they are the first known instance of a “Five Eyes” country (referring to the Australia, Canada, Upcoming Zealand, the U.K. and the U.S.) sanctioning a cryptocurrency operation incorporated in another Five Eyes jurisdiction.

Where do entities like Cryptomus and Heleket derive their authority to offer international financial services? The answer appears to involve fake financial institutions overseen by a phony regulatory body positioned in a country that is not widely recognized as a sovereign nation.

Our 2024 investigation found the sole shareholder of Cryptomus’s parent company Certa Payments was a 25-year-old Ukrainian woman who also headed several other firms, including the WS Management and Advisory Corporation, which bills itself as the regulatory body that exclusively oversees licenses for cryptocurrency, foreign exchange and online gaming businesses incorporated in the disputed region in northwest Africa known as the Western Sahara.

That entity’s website — crasadr.com — says it assists applicants with bank setup and formation, online gaming licenses, and the creation and licensing of foreign exchange brokers. One of Certa Payments’ former sites — certa[.]website — also shared a server with 12 other domains, including rasd-state[.]ws, a website for the Central Reserve Authority of the Western Sahara.

The website crasadr dot com, the official website of the Central Reserve Authority of Western Sahara, which lists the entities awarded licenses for cryptocurrencies, gaming and foreign exchange services.

📅 29 Oct 2026 • ⏱️ 8m • 📚 Deep Dive (1572 w)

Welcome Le Chonk: Mistral Large 4 on Hugging Face

📅 29 Oct 2026 | ⏱️ 8 min read (1572 words, 📚 Deep Dive) | Source: Hugging Face

⏱️ ~8 mins left to finish
📖 0% read
💡 Key Takeaways
  • Mistral Large 4 (aka Le Chonk) is a multimodal, multilingual, Mixture-of-Experts (MoE) model from Mistral.
  • There are also GGUFs created by Unsloth and the llama.cpp team.
  • It has been revealed that mistral Large 4 is particularly strong for cybersecurity, coding agents, and multimodality.
📑 Quick Jump: 1. Overview • 2. Key Details • 3. Closing Notes

Mistral Large 4 (aka Le Chonk) is a multimodal, multilingual, Mixture-of-Experts (MoE) model from Mistral. It takes text and images as input and generates text. It has about 1T total, 49B active parameter, and a context window of 1M tokens.

The model is released in two official variants:.

There are also GGUFs created by Unsloth and the llama.cpp team. It’s distributed under the Mistral Ecosystem Open-Weight License (an MIT derivative that establishes limitations for model-as-a-service offerings).

It has been revealed that mistral Large 4 is particularly strong for cybersecurity, coding agents, and multimodality. In this post, we look at how the model works, its capabilities, architecture and more!

Mistral Large 4 combines a large pool of experts with sparse attention and a Pixtral vision encoder. The language model selects a small group of experts for each token, while its attention indexer selects which earlier token positions to attend to. These are two different forms of sparsity, where one selects feed-forward networks, the other selects context positions.

You can find all the checkpoints in the Mistral Large 4 collection.

Industry observers note that mistral Large 4 scores 82% on the Artificial Analysis Cyber Index test that asks a model to reproduce a real vulnerability in open-source software and then patch the software. Mistral reports that several closed frontier models score near zero on the same test because they refuse to attempt the work. This is super notable for defenders, because fixing a vulnerability usually requires reproducing the vulnerability. In Mistral’s internal testing, Mistral Large 4 was also useful for malware analysis, vulnerability prioritisation and writing detection rules, which the model was not explicitly trained for.

Mistral mainly positions the model for defensive security work. Vulnerability research and incident response often appear like attacks in model input, so closed source filters can block them. A team that depends on an API can also lose access in the middle of an incident. Crucially, open weight models put both the usage policy and the deployment under the user’s control. That said, the model still declines harmful requests: on cyber prompts from JailbreakBench, StrongREJECT and AgentHarm, its average refusal rate is higher than any other open weight model.

For community builders, an open weight model like Mistral Large 4 unlocks a load of downstream use cases. You could build your own cyber system around your code base, crash logs, and malware samples. For example, with TRL you could fine-tune smaller models from Mistral Large 4 traces patching your code base. In fact, reproduce-then-patch tasks use a verifiable reward, so it fits with RL environments that could be used to further RL smaller security models. Open weights also let researchers measure the model’s refusal behaviour directly instead of relying on the provider’s description.

In short, cyber capabilities like ML4’s in the open are a huge boost for the community.

We have interviewed Pierre Stock about the cyber capabilities of the model, you can watch it here.

Mistral Large 4’s text decoder has 72 layers, a hidden dimension of 6,144, and 64 attention heads. Its attention blocks combine Multi-head Latent Attention (MLA) with a DeepSeek Sparse Attention (DSA) indexer (a direction in other models such as GLM 5.3). MLA keeps a compressed KV representation, and DSA selects up to 2,048 key positions for each query.

For each decoder block, there’s a 3:1 RoPE to NoPE pattern, i.e. 3 decoder layers employ RoPE and every fourth layer uses NoPE. The model also shares KV state across layers.The first decoder layer uses a dense feed-forward network. The other 71 layers use MoE blocks, in which a softmax router selects four of the 128 experts for each token. One shared expert always runs alongside the selected experts, for a total of 5 active experts per token.

Regarding RoPE, Mistral uses LeRope, a YaRN-scaled RoPE with one learned multiplier per frequency.

Industry observers note that mistral Large 4 employs a 1.6B Pixtral encoder. Pixtral has 30 layers, a hidden dimension of 2,048, and 16 attention heads. It uses 14 × 14 patches and a patch-merge projector with spatial merge size 2. You can see the encoder pipeline below.

In a recent development, mistral Large 4 delivers strong benchmark performance across coding, cybersecurity, multimodal understanding, and agentic workflows, positioning it as a competitive addition to the open-weight ecosystem. As of October 29, 2026, the model is the fifth best open weights model on Artificial Analysis Intelligence index.

On coding, ML4 achieves 61.7% on DeepSWE v1.1, 59.4% on SWE-Atlas-QnA, and 28.3% on Terminal-Bench 4. Its combined Coding Agent Index score of 49.8% places it ahead of DeepSeek V4 Pro 0813 and Qwen3.8 Max.

Coding capabilities of ML4 extend to knowledge work, with 59.9% on AutomationBench and 1,393 Elo on AA-Briefcase, which evaluate business workflows and long-horizon professional tasks.

Cybersecurity is one of Mistral Large 4’s standout capabilities, with strong results across real-world vulnerability assessment and security competition tasks. Three benchmarks highlight the model’s cyber performance:.

Industry observers note that mistral Large 4 also demonstrates 93.3% attack resistance on Lakera’s B3 benchmark, adding evidence of robustness against prompt-injection attacks. Beyond benchmarks, internal testing highlighted promising results in malware analysis, vulnerability prioritization, and detection-rule generation.

The default is high, and note that reasoning cannot be disabled, so using reasoning_effort: none would still use high.

Breaking: Announcing Project ProtoStar: Making Publicly Funded Science AI-Ready

📅 29 Oct 2026 | ⏱️ 6 min read (1291 words, 📚 Deep Dive) | Source: Hugging Face

⏱️ ~6 mins left to finish
📖 0% read
💡 Key Takeaways
  • An initiative bringing together universities, research organizations, industry, and the open science community to make publicly funded research easier to discover, reuse, and build upon.
  • Today, we're announcing Project ProtoStar, an initiative to unlock the potential of publicly funded scientific research by making datasets, models, and code more accessible and reusable, particularly for AI-driven research.
  • The initiative's founding partners include Carnegie Mellon University, Purdue University, Georgia Institute of Technology, Arizona State University, and The George Washington University, all working through the Open Forum for AI (OFAI) as the university coalition partner; the Astera Institute; Hugging Face as the infrastructure partner; and the Open Research Community Accelerator (ORCA), through its Fostering Innovation Network, as the community partner.
📑 Quick Jump: 1. Overview • 2. Key Details • 3. Closing Notes

An initiative bringing together universities, research organizations, industry, and the open science community to make publicly funded research easier to discover, reuse, and build upon.

Today, we're announcing Project ProtoStar, an initiative to unlock the potential of publicly funded scientific research by making datasets, models, and code more accessible and reusable, particularly for AI-driven research. ProtoStar brings together research institutions, industry, and the open science community to support the release of scientific artifacts in AI-ready, machine-actionable formats, and to demonstrate their value through a series of open challenges. The first challenge, hosted by Carnegie Mellon University, opens on November 2. See How to Participate below.

The initiative's founding partners include Carnegie Mellon University, Purdue University, Georgia Institute of Technology, Arizona State University, and The George Washington University, all working through the Open Forum for AI (OFAI) as the university coalition partner; the Astera Institute; Hugging Face as the infrastructure partner; and the Open Research Community Accelerator (ORCA), through its Fostering Innovation Network, as the community partner.

In a recent development, participating organizations formalize their involvement through a memorandum of understanding supporting the release of suitable scientific datasets, models, and code in AI-ready formats on open infrastructure. Organizations interested in joining Project ProtoStar can reach out to protostar@orcaopen.org.

The U.S. federal government invests approximately $190 billion annually in research and development, and federal policy increasingly expects the results to be shared publicly. Agencies such as the National Institutes of Health (NIH) and National Science Foundation (NSF) have strengthened public-access requirements for funded research publications and require researchers to initiative for sharing the underlying data. Hugging Face is among the ten generalist repositories listed by NIH for sharing research data.

It has been revealed that but making research publicly available does not automatically make it usable. Scientific datasets, models, and code are often scattered across incompatible systems, stored in static or legacy formats, or released without the documentation, metadata, and provenance needed to understand and reuse them. These limitations make it harder for researchers to build on existing work, and harder still for AI systems to discover, interpret, and combine scientific resources across disciplines.

Project ProtoStar aims to help close this gap by encouraging systematic sharing of publicly funded scientific artifacts in AI-ready formats, supported by open infrastructure and practical publishing guidance. It builds on efforts such as the National Cancer Institute's AI Data-Readiness Challenge and Hugging Face's guide to preparing public-sector data for AI. The goal is to make it easier for research organizations to meet existing public-access expectations while increasing the scientific value of the work they release.

The demand for reusable scientific resources is already evident. Hugging Face hosts more than 17,000 public datasets across core scientific domains, including genomics, protein design, chemistry, weather and climate, Earth observation, and astronomy. That figure approaches 29,000 when medicine and mathematics are included, alongside a comparable number of scientific models.

The pace of sharing is also accelerating. Researchers shared more than three times as many new science datasets on Hugging Face in the first nine months of 2026 as in the same period of 2025, with growth remaining substantial even after excluding the largest individual uploader.

It has been revealed that figure 1. Upcoming public science datasets on Hugging Face per quarter, by domain (Q1 2023–Q3 2026). Counts datasets still public, by creation date. Source: Hugging Face Hub data, October 2026. Explore the data.

When organizations share research in reusable formats, the scientific community can build on it at scale. The 18 public repositories maintained by NIH's National Center for Biotechnology Information (NCBI) on Hugging Face have collectively received more than 11 million downloads, while NASA IMPACT's 27 repositories have received approximately 770,000 downloads, as of October 26, 2026. Documentation is also an crucial part of making these resources useful: 90% of dataset downloads on Hugging Face are from fully documented datasets.

Publicly available genomic data has proved important in contributing to research that further advances fields such as biological research; researchers at Hugging Face have been building on openly available scientific resources, including recent releases from HuggingFaceBio such as Carbon-A and Carbon-X. By releasing the resulting models, datasets, and tools openly, these efforts demonstrate how existing scientific resources can support new research that others can build upon.

This is the kind of activity that we are further catalyzing via Project ProtoStar through institutional policies adopted by participating orgs. As an early example of institutional commitment, CMU's Open Source Programs Office is encouraging its researchers to share suitable datasets, AI models, and other research outputs on Hugging Face, while recognizing the continued importance of domain-specific repositories.

Industry observers note that making scientific artifacts AI-ready is an important first step. We also want to demonstrate what researchers, developers, and the broader scientific community can accomplish when those resources are made available for reuse.

A central question for ProtoStar is: Can publicly funded scientific datasets, models, and code, released in AI-ready formats, be readily discovered, reused, combined, and extended to accelerate scientific discovery and public benefit?

To explore this, ProtoStar will organize a series of open challenges, each hosted by a participating research institution and built around scientific resources that the institution has released openly. The challenges have two complementary goals:.

The resulting projects and lessons learned will help build a practical evidence base for making publicly funded science more accessible and useful.

Hosted by Carnegie Mellon University | November 2–13, 2026.

In a recent development, the inaugural ProtoStar challenge invites participants to test whether AI can improve predictions of urban climate conditions using historical weather data from 210 U.S. cities. Building on research by Carnegie Mellon University, teams will use climate records through 2018 to predict actual conditions from 2019 to 2026, allowing their models to be evaluated against observed weather rather than hypothetical future scenarios.

Participants will forecast four indicators relevant to urban planning: average annual temperature, total annual precipitation, the hottest day of the year, and cooling degree days, a measure of demand for air conditioning. Their predictions will be compared against simple statistical baselines, including historical averages and linear trends, to assess whether AI approaches offer meaningful improvements in accuracy.

Beyond forecasting, participants will also propose a short climate adaptation policy idea informed by what they learned from the data. This component encourages teams to connect scientific analysis with practical public benefits, such as preparing cities for extreme heat, improving energy efficiency, or managing changing precipitation patterns.

In a recent development, teams will submit a Hugging Face dataset with these outputs. Forecasting performance will be assessed through a public leaderboard measuring prediction errors against established baselines, while policy ideas will receive separate consideration. Final forecasting results will be published in early 2027, once the complete 2026 weather records are available.

Explore the CMU Climate Risk Intelligence Challenge.

The CMU challenge is the first in this series. Other participating institutions will host their own challenges sequentially, each highlighting different publicly funded scientific resources and opportunities for reuse. Future challenges will be unveiled through the Project ProtoStar page on Hugging Face.

Whether you're an academic researcher, student, independent developer, or company building on open scientific infrastructure, ProtoStar offers opportunities to put publicly funded research to work and help us learn what is needed to make AI-ready open science more widely useful.

Recent findings suggest that we also welcome universities, federal research agencies, national laboratories, nonprofits, and other research organizations interested in making their scientific resources more accessible and reusable. To explore participation or collaboration, reach out to protostar@orcaopen.org.

Our hope is that ProtoStar will make it easier for publicly funded scientific work to reach the people and tools that can build on it, while generating practical evidence about the infrastructure and practices needed to support open science at scale.

Latest Update: Feds Suspect Ransom Negotiator Ran ShinyHunters Extortion Site

📅 19 Oct 2026 | ⏱️ 13 min read (2557 words, 📚 Deep Dive) | Source: Krebsonsecurity

⏱️ ~13 mins left to finish

💡 Key Takeaways
  • federal investigators pursuing the ShinyHunters hacking group that recently stole highly sensitive data from the FBI have identified executives at two different ransomware negotiation firms who maintained unusually close relations with the extortion group, KrebsOnSecurity has learned.
  • Hackers aligned with ShinyHunters have claimed credit for dozens of major data breaches since 2019, when the group was primarily operated by cybercriminals living in France.
  • In late September, ShinyHunters hacked the FBI recruitment website fbijobs.gov and taunted the agency by threatening to publish the stolen files, which reportedly included medical and psychological records, Social Security numbers and home addresses, and information about each employee’s unit and specialization.
📑 Quick Jump: 1. Overview • 2. Key Details • 3. Closing Notes

Recent findings suggest that U.S. federal investigators pursuing the ShinyHunters hacking group that recently stole highly sensitive data from the FBI have identified executives at two different ransomware negotiation firms who maintained unusually close relations with the extortion group, KrebsOnSecurity has learned. Sources close to the investigation say one of the executives in the United States even helped ShinyHunters operate a website that pressured victims into paying a ransom.

Hackers aligned with ShinyHunters have claimed credit for dozens of major data breaches since 2019, when the group was primarily operated by cybercriminals living in France. As those original members were arrested or jailed one by one, control over the ShinyHunters brand eventually passed to “Rey,” identified last year as a teenage hacker from Amman, Jordan. According to the FBI, ShinyHunters has extorted more than $70 million from victims so far this year.

In late September, ShinyHunters hacked the FBI recruitment website fbijobs.gov and taunted the agency by threatening to publish the stolen files, which reportedly included medical and psychological records, Social Security numbers and home addresses, and information about each employee’s unit and specialization.

Recent findings suggest that the FBI jobs site hack has prompted the agency to move with uncommon speed to arrest, detain and question people who had any communications with Rey or other ShinyHunters suspects. Reuters reported on October 3 that Rey had been detained by Jordanian authorities and was cooperating with the FBI.

Rey was able to assume control over the hacking group because one of its alleged senior members had just been nabbed. On the evening of September 15, 2026, authorities in the Netherlands arrested convicted hacker and ShinyHunters suspect Pepijn van der Stap. Dutch police reportedly used flash-bang grenades in an effort to stun and apprehend Van der Stap as he was logged in to various online accounts.

According to a source close to the investigation, the authorities arrested Van der Stap while he was using his Signal instant messaging account, which allowed them to read recent communications with frequent contacts — including ransomware negotiators based in Canada and the United States.

Multiple sources with knowledge of the matter told KrebsOnSecurity that Van der Stap’s messages were the key to unraveling a murder-for-hire plot that emerged immediately following his arrest. The Dutch news outlet RTL reported last month the two murders were allegedly to be committed abroad, and that there are indications Van der Stap gave the order for the attacks (there is no indication those orders were ever carried out).

On October 9, KrebsOnSecurity broke the news that the FBI arrested a 54-year-old Canadian cybersecurity executive named Edward Dubrovsky in connection with the ShinyHunters investigation. Dubrovsky, who recently published a book on handling cyber extortion that recommended always engaging with the hackers, was charged with threatening to disclose stolen or hacked data and interfering with interstate commerce through extortion, according to court records. Politico reports prosecutors have asked that Dubrovsky remain in custody pending trial, and that records related to his case remain under seal.

Sources indicate that A source close to the investigation told KrebsOnSecurity that Van der Stap’s Signal messages revealed he had frequent conversations with Mr. Dubrovsky and with at least one executive at a large U.S.-based consulting firm, and that these executives often knew the details about newly introduced ShinyHunters victims before the victims themselves had even learned of the breach.

That source shared another potentially explosive finding by federal investigators: the Dutch hacker’s chats showed Mr. Dubrovsky knew ShinyHunters had stolen highly sensitive data from FBI servers, and that he never informed the bureau of the data breach prior to ShinyHunters threatening on Twitter/X to publish the agency’s deeply personal personnel files.

KrebsOnSecurity has learned from two sources close to the ShinyHunters probe that FBI investigators believe at least one executive at a U.S.-based consulting firm played an active role in operating the now-defunct ShinyHunters victim extortion website “shinywire[.]com.” KrebsOnSecurity is not naming the U.S. company or the suspected executive(s) for now because they have not yet been charged with a crime, but it is a prestigious firm with more than 1,000 associates.

A section of the homepage for the now-defunct Shinywire website.

Recent findings suggest that the Shinywire website was active from approximately May 3, 2026 until October 16 and had entries for nearly 100 organizations hacked by ShinyHunters. Each entry urged victims to engage with the cybercrime group and discuss terms for payment. The pages also included samples of stolen files and promised those files would be published online if the victim ignored their demands.

The following screenshot reveals a cached portion of the Shinywire extortion page for Intuitive Surgical, an American medical technology company that was breached in March 2026 after an employee fell for a targeted phishing email.

Industry observers note that the Shinywire website, as indexed by urlscan.io. This listing is an extortion demand targeting Intuitive Surgical, an American medical technology company breached in March 2026 by a targeted phishing email attack that compromised an employee’s credentials.

Victim organizations that refused to engage or negotiate after seven days would find all of their stolen data published on the ShinyHunters victim shaming blog (a website that is only reachable via the anonymity network Tor).

In a story published October 15, The Globe and Mail wrote that a few months before Edward Dubrovsky was arrested by the FBI, the Canadian cybersecurity executive alleged in court documents he had become collateral damage in a campaign by a former business partner to “destroy” another industry executive.

The story noted that Dubrovsky filed the lawsuit in Ontario this year against Daniel Tobok, the former chief executive of Cypfer, a cybersecurity firm founded in Toronto with offices in the U.S., Britain, the Netherlands, the United Arab Emirates, and Mexico. The two first became business partners in 2017 and later developed Cypfer together, where Mr. Dubrovsky was a managing partner and chief operating officer. But by 2024, the two had a falling out, with Dubrovsky accusing Tobok of gradually excluding him from business matters and making “increasingly capricious business decisions.”.

In a recent development, mr. Tobok reportedly denied the allegations and filed a counterclaim, accusing Mr. Dubrovsky of accessing confidential information and unfairly competing with Cypfer through work at another firm called CyberSteward Inc. He also mentioned Mr. Dubrovsky has misrepresented himself as a Cypfer founder, and is not a shareholder.

According to interviews with several former colleagues of Mr. Tobok, as far back as eight years ago he was known to ransomware purveyors by a particular nickname: Ghostbyte. In 2018, a Canadian firm was hacked by Dharma, a prolific Russian-language ransomware affiliate program that first surfaced in 2016. The victim company told the Dharma ransomware representative they were leaning toward paying because some of the files were unrecoverable after being locked, but that they needed a better guarantee that Dharma would keep their word if paid.

A redacted copy of the Dharma rep’s reply is pictured below, and it indicates the ransomware group urged the victim to contact a person at a Canadian IT firm that helps companies seeking such guarantees. The Dharma rep recommended the victim contact the email address ghostbyte@tutanota.com.

“If you want guarantees, you can write to the IT company,” the Dharma reply advised. “Take the phone and negotiate with them. This IT company often solves such problems in Canada. You can contact them and sign a contract for services. You’ll still have to pay.”.

An email reply from the Dharma ransomware group to a victim, recommending they contact an email address that is connected to Mr. Tobok.

It has been revealed that it’s unclear if Mr. Tobok ever used that Ghostbyte address offered by the Dharma representative, and he has not responded to multiple requests for comment. However, the breach tracking service Constella Intelligence finds an email address Mr. Tobok has frequently used — dtobok@me.com — is associated with two online accounts where the chosen username was “ghostbyte,” including a Snapchat account.

Incidentally, Constella also finds the Dharma rep’s email address luckygoodlucky@tuta.io is associated with a cryptocurrency address that processed 38 transactions totaling 43 bitcoin, ~$3.5 million at today’s value (the most recent transaction for this wallet is dated February 2019).

In a statement shared on October 14, Cypfer said the manufacturer’s business does not include making or facilitating ransomware payments, and that Cypfer learned of Dubrovsky’s arrest when the news first broke in the media.

In a recent development, “We had no prior knowledge of Mr. Dubrovsky’s arrest,” a spokesperson told KrebsOnSecurity via email. “CYPFER has not received any outreach from law enforcement and, to our knowledge, is not the target of any law enforcement investigation.”.

The statement said CyberSteward and Cypfer are separate companies with no officers, directors or employees in common, and that Cypfer was recently acquired by the Apros Group, a holding firm led by Jason Hogg, a former FBI special agent and former CEO of Aon Cyber Solutions Group. In 2020, Aon aquired Cytelligence, a security consulting firm where Mr. Tobok was founder and CEO and Mr. Dubrovsky was a managing partner.

It is not illegal in the United States to pay hackers for an encryption key to unlock servers infected with ransomware, or in exchange for a promise to delete any stolen files and refrain from publishing them online. While victim organizations can land in legal hot water if they pay a ransom to a group that is sanctioned by the U.S. Treasury Department, ShinyHunters is not among the ransomware groups right now sanctioned by the United States or by any other government.

Recent findings suggest that experts say ransomware victims are typically directed by their insurance provider to work with a specific incident response firm. But not all cyber forensics and breach response companies will agree to facilitate payments to ransomware groups on behalf of their clients. As a result, once victim firms make a decision to pay, the firms that eschew rewarding extortionists are invariably replaced by companies that have no such qualms.

In December 2024, ShinyHunters began extorting the education technology company PowerSchool, stealing private information on 62 million students and 9.5 million teachers in the U.S. and Canada. PowerSchool reportedly paid a $2.85 million ransom demand, and a “frequently asked questions” statement (PDF) about the breach says PowerSchool was assisted in that effort by CyberSteward (ShinyHunters affiliate Matthew Lane, 20, of Sterling, Mass., was sentenced in November 2025 to four years in prison for his admitted role in the PowerSchool hack).

Industry observers note that but that ransom payment did not stop future extortion attempts using the same stolen data. By May 2025, individual school districts were reportedly receiving separate ransom demands using samples of the same stolen files. While nobody has alleged ShinyHunters was behind the second wave of extortion against PowerSchool users, the incident drives home the reality that there is no technical way to verify the threat actors have deleted the stolen data as promised, or prevent others from abusing the same records.

A number of leading cyber incident response firms, including Coveware and Unit 221B, have consistently warned victims against paying ShinyHunters, noting that “destroyed” victim data is often kept, resold or used to extort the manufacturer’s clients directly later on.

The FBI echoed those sentiments in an alert on May 15, 2026 advising victims against paying the ShinyHunters group. Meanwhile, ShinyHunters members have been harassing and threatening employees at Coveware and Unit 221B for offering this advice.

Sources indicate that the following screenshots show just how annoyed the ShinyHunters leaders were with Coveware’s relentless advice against paying the group. The first image is from a conversation on May 6, 2026 that took place between the group’s main account on Telegram and a co-conspirator. In that chat, snippets of which were shared with KrebsOnSecurity by a trusted source, ShinyHunters complained that Coveware was harming the group’s payment rates.

The operator of the ShinyHunters account on Telegram speaking privately with a co-conspirator and complaining that Coveware was harming their business.

“Go on my website, majority of those companies would’ve paid if it weren’t for Coveware giving them misinformation,” the ShinyHunters account wrote. “Someone (100% Coveware) is going out of their way to make sure i am not paid.”.

It has been revealed that in another conversation on April 11, 2026, the ShinyHunters Telegram account privately stated they were trying to “eliminate the problem,” which they said was Coveware. Coveware declined to comment for this story.

“I’m sure the company will pay but in this specific case I am aware of Coveware and their involvement, and I’ve probably been not getting a lot of other negotiations mostly likely because Coveware keeps getting involved,” the ShinyHunters account bemoaned.

The operator of the ShinyHunters account on Telegram telling a co-conspirator they were “trying to eliminate the problem,” which they identified as Coveware advising victims not to pay the cybercrime group.

Industry observers note that mark Camillo is chief executive at CyberAcuView, an industry group founded in 2021 by a consortium of major cyber insurance carriers. Camillo said some firms charge a flat retainer fee, while those that specialize in helping companies negotiate a ransom payment tend to charge a percentage of the total ransom amount paid.

That latter dynamic, he stated, is an inherent conflict of interest, as the negotiator has every incentive to make things more favorable to the attackers because they are financially incentivized to negotiate and pay out, and to not negotiate down on the price.

In a recent development, “It has come to the industry’s attention that many of the ransomware payers charge a percentage of the final payment which may or may not be disclosed,” Camillo stated. “This makes no sense if they are also the negotiator. There needs to be more transparency in the process as no one in the ecosystem should be profiting purely on the size of the ransomware transaction or payment itself.”.

Camillo said the firms doing this work would argue the fees are needed because there may be unexpectedly higher costs to secure larger quantities of cryptocurrency or more risk carrying the float, and because cryptocurrency exchanges may charge higher fees for high risk transactions.

“There definitely needs to be more visibility around the transaction and clarity on the increasing value of the crypto and the exchange’s percent in the transaction to get to the bottom of this and remove any misaligned incentives,” he said.

Recent findings suggest that in recent months, the U.S. Department of Justice has prosecuted a number of ransomware negotiators alleged to have conspired with cybercriminals to defraud their clients. On October 7, the DOJ charged MonsterCloud CEO Zohar Pinhasi, 50, with wire fraud and conspiracy for allegedly charging customers to remediate ransomware attacks without paying the hackers. According to charging documents, Pinhasi secretly went behind his customers’ backs and paid hackers anyway, paying ransomware groups $8 million while charging customers $19 million.

Recent findings suggest that in July, Angelo Martino, a 41-year-old ransomware negotiator from Land O’Lakes, Florida, was sentenced to 70 months in prison for conspiring with the Blackcat/ALPHV ransomware group to extort multiple victims. According to the DOJ, Martino was paid by BlackCat attackers to provide confidential information about the negotiating position and strategy of his employer’s clients and enable the ransomware actors to maximize the ransoms paid by the victims.

⏱️ ~4 mins left to finish
📖 0% read
💡 Key Takeaways
  • Expect to see quite a few websites serving error pages today: Nearly 70 percent of websites need to update their core software to fix a pair of vulnerabilities that allow an attacker to seize full control over affected servers.
  • According to recent reports, the flaws at problem are present in PHP, the programming language that powers sites running on a large number of web publishing systems, including Drupal, Magento, Joomla and WordPress.
  • Reuters reports that government websites in Europe and elsewhere went offline today after the PHP vulnerabilities were disclosed.
📑 Quick Jump: 1. Overview • 2. Key Details • 3. Closing Notes

Expect to see quite a few websites serving error pages today: Nearly 70 percent of websites need to update their core software to fix a pair of vulnerabilities that allow an attacker to seize full control over affected servers. Experts say there are working exploits for the flaws, and that these critical bugs are already being exploited in the wild.

Image: Shutterstock.com, Sashkin.

According to recent reports, the flaws at problem are present in PHP, the programming language that powers sites running on a large number of web publishing systems, including Drupal, Magento, Joomla and WordPress. Earlier today, PHP released an emergency security update to fix two critical bugs that can allow an attacker to execute code of their choosing on a vulnerable server.

Reuters reports that government websites in Europe and elsewhere went offline today after the PHP vulnerabilities were disclosed. Cloudflare remarked it has already detected some exploitation of the flaw, and that at 3:02 am (UTC) it implemented web application firewall rules to protect websites from attack traffic seeking to exploit the bugs, which could cause a denial of service condition, remote code execution, and data exposure.

OpenAI, which was involved in the vulnerability research and outreach, said “given the severity of these flaws and PHP’s widespread use, we consider this one of the most impactful security challenges in recent memory.”.

Censys, a company that tracks the technology used by Internet hosts, said a recent scan identified approximately 2.58 million Internet facing hosts and 54.9 million web properties running PHP.

Security experts at Wiz mentioned every PHP version released in the last decade is affected by at least one of these vulnerabilities [full disclosure: Wiz is an advertiser on this blog].

It has been revealed that “These findings rank among the most severe vulnerabilities discovered in PHP, and arguably in software history,” reads a blog post published today by a team of researchers at Wiz, which was one of several organizations credited with discovering the vulnerabilities. “The underlying flaws had been present for decades, but demonstrating their exploitability required an exceptionally complex chain of steps, at the edge of what human researchers could practically achieve. Frontier AI models substantially reduced that barrier, turning a longstanding flaw into an exploit.”.

It has been revealed that the Wiz researchers say it is likely the PHP vulnerabilities will be mass-exploited to install web-based backdoors or “web shells,” which give attackers a web-based panel that allows them to remotely control infected sites. Wiz noted that prior to the PHP bugs being publicly disclosed, the organization worked with the PHP team, Calif and OpenAI to measure the size of the problem and coordinate patch verification and disclosure.

According to recent reports, the PHP zero-day vulnerabilities are being tracked by their CVE numbers, CVE-2026-109618 and CVE-2026-109619, and they affect all web servers running PHP 5.4 or later. The bugs are fixed in PHP 8.5.12, 8.4.27, 8.3.36, and 8.2.35.

According to Wiz, PHP is so deeply embedded in many web applications that we are likely to see organizations struggling to patch these vulnerabilities for some time to come, comparing this PHP vulnerability pair with the Log4Shell weakness that emerged in 2021 — a widespread, severe-as-it-gets security flaw in Log4j, a popular Java logging framework.

“A vulnerability in core PHP reaches far beyond a single application,” the Wiz researchers wrote. “PHP runs across clouds, hosting providers, content-delivery networks and millions of independently managed servers. Reducing exposure before the technical details became public required coordinated work across that entire ecosystem.”.

The SANS Internet Storm Center is keeping an eye on major software platforms that are shipping updates to deal with these PHP flaws. For example, Ubuntu just released updated PHP packages. For a technical deep-dive on these vulnerabilities that tells the timeline of the discovery of these bugs in a comic book style, check out this post from Calif, another technology tech giant credited with finding the PHP flaws.

A snapshot of php2shell.censys.com, the website Censys set up to track the PHP vulnerabilities.

Industry observers note that this is a fast-moving story. Updates will be noted here with timestamps.

Tech Firms Dismantle Botnet That Turned 1.3M TV Boxes Into Proxies

📅 03 Nov 2026 | ⏱️ 6 min read (1240 words, 📚 Deep Dive) | Source: Krebsonsecurity

⏱️ ~6 mins left to finish
📖 0% read
💡 Key Takeaways
  • In a recent development, google stated today it worked with industry partners to dismantle a botnet made up of more than 1.3 million Android TV set-top boxes that ship with malicious software which secretly rents the user’s Internet connection out to strangers and conducts advertising fraud.
  • A report from the Google Threat Intelligence Group (GTIG) noted Google has severed ties with Videostrong Technology Co., a TV box manufacturer in China that GTIG and other industry experts concluded was responsible for including malware that enrolled more than 1.3 million set-top boxes in a botnet dubbed “XCPE” (named after one of the malware’s core code components).
  • In a recent development, the global distribution of XCPE botnet infections.
📑 Quick Jump: 1. Overview • 2. Key Details • 3. Closing Notes

In a recent development, google stated today it worked with industry partners to dismantle a botnet made up of more than 1.3 million Android TV set-top boxes that ship with malicious software which secretly rents the user’s Internet connection out to strangers and conducts advertising fraud. Experts involved in the takedown say the action is likely to sever the botnet’s access to more than 10 million additional compromised systems, including other Internet of Things (IoT) products such as Android-based healthcare devices and karaoke machines.

A report from the Google Threat Intelligence Group (GTIG) noted Google has severed ties with Videostrong Technology Co., a TV box manufacturer in China that GTIG and other industry experts concluded was responsible for including malware that enrolled more than 1.3 million set-top boxes in a botnet dubbed “XCPE” (named after one of the malware’s core code components).

In a recent development, the global distribution of XCPE botnet infections. Image: Google Threat Intelligence Group.

It has been revealed that the report said the XCPE botnet loaded the user’s device with software that makes their Internet address available for resale by multiple “residential proxy” services, which allow customers to rent Internet addresses as a way to anonymize their web traffic or spoof their true location. As detailed in several stories here over the past year, residential proxy services are a major source of unwanted and often malicious traffic, including account takeover activity, advertising fraud, and mass content scraping for AI projects.

“Videostrong monetized the backdoor by selling access to criminal affiliates and loading those affiliates’ malware modules onto infected devices,” the GTIG post reads, noting that Google took legal action to take down the domains and servers Videostrong used to control the botnet and install additional malware. “A device manufacturer intentionally infecting their users with malware is an unacceptable breach of trust, and represents a serious risk to those users. Without users’ knowledge or consent, infected devices were offered as a distribution mechanism for a wide array of criminal actors.”.

The report notes that while TV boxes made up the the majority of the botnet, the same XCPE malware was found in other Android-based IoT products, including telehealth devices, karaoke machines, and even digital signage systems.

Google noted it requires all Android device makers to pass compatibility and security tests to ensure their products don’t harm users, but that Videostrong nevertheless found a way to load their malicious software immediately after a user boots up one of these devices for the first time (Google says it has since addressed that weakness).

Sources indicate that the GTIG report calls out a number of residential proxy providers whose software development kits were routinely downloaded by devices infected by the XCPE botnet. Those include AppSalt, also known as Honeygain, which was developed by the Vilnius, Lithuania-based Oxylabs. In October 2026, Oxylabs and Honeygain were reorganized as independent platforms under an umbrella entity called Source, which received $130 million in funding from private equity firm Warburg Pincus that reportedly valued the business at $3.6 billion.

According to recent reports, another provider linked to the botnet was NetNut, a once sprawling residential proxy company operated by the publicly-traded Israeli company Alarum Technologies. In July 2026, the FBI worked with industry partners to seize hundreds of domains associated with NetNut, saying the company was responsible for operating a separate botnet called Popa that enslaved TV boxes as residential proxies. Other proxy providers named in the GTIG report include EarnFM, Traffmonetizer, Jaguar, LINKFOG, BMW/IPWeb and GaGaNode.

According to recent reports, google’s announcement credits a number of industry partners, including Synthient, a startup that tracks proxy providers. In January 2026, Synthient published research into the rapid spread of the Kimwolf botnet, which at the time was hammering networks worldwide with record-smashing DDoS attacks. Synthient documented how Kimwolf infected millions of Android set-top boxes virtually overnight, using a widespread vulnerability in these residential proxy services to compromise other Android-based devices inside the local networks of unsuspecting TV box consumers.

Synthient’s research caused dozens of residential proxy providers to patch their networks, which helped to fragment the Kimwolf botnet into much smaller pieces that made its incessant and disruptive DDoS attacks far easier for network operators to manage. It also attracted the attention of the Motion Picture Association (MPA), a trade group representing the major Hollywood studios, which partnered with Synthient to purchase and tear apart a number of popular Android TV set-top boxes — including some that were being infected by Kimwolf and other IoT botnets.

It has been revealed that in a report published today, Synthient examined a popular, pre-infected TV box sold under the brand MECOOL by a publicly traded firm in China called Skyworth Technology, concluding that MECOOL also bundled the malware from Videostrong Technology Co. and likewise installed AppSalt/Honeygain and other proxy components.

The MECOOL storefront and marketing. Image: Synthient.com.

Industry observers note that synthient founder Ben Brundage told KrebsOnSecurity that Videostrong’s malware also distributed software for the proxy service Grass. In our November 2025 story, “Is Your Android TV Streaming Box Part of a Botnet?” we quoted a researcher from Censys who found the popular Superbox TV streaming device bundled Grass’s residential proxy software. We also quoted the Grass founder, who denied any affiliation with the TV box maker.

That November 2025 story noted that Superbox and similar Android TV set-top boxes gain fresh customers primarily by engaging influencers on Tiktok and other social networks who praise the product’s ability to offer hundreds of (pirated) pay TV streaming services for a one-time fee.

The popular Youtube channel Linus Tech Tips discussing MECOOL TV streaming boxes.

The GTIG report estimates the XCPE botnet takedown should sever access to at least 10 million additional compromised devices, noting that the various proxy and ad fraud affiliates of Videostrong “each have diversified distribution channels for their modules beyond XCPE.”.

Synthient’s Brundage echoed that conclusion, calling the 1.3 million number “highly conservative.”.

Industry observers note that “The scale of affected devices is likely way higher,” he noted. “This is probably the largest operation against backdoored TV boxes that we’ve seen.”.

It has been revealed that revision, Nov. 5, 11:07 a.m. ET: In a statement shared post-publication, Oxylabs stated that while its system is built so that a device can’t be used as a proxy exit node unless they receive a signal that it has consented, the developer faked these signals.

“We have been conducting regular audits of the applications provided by our partners,” the statement reads. “However, following this incident, we will improve the application and application’s build fingerprinting logic to better detect cases where the SDK is running on an unapproved build of an originally authorized application.”.

The statement mentioned Oxylabs has no record of any company called Videostrong Technology Co., but it did find between is suppliers the domain “com.abc[.]nexus,” mentioned in the GTIG report as an external malware loader.

Recent findings suggest that “As soon as we saw that, we suspended the relationship and sent them a formal legal inquiry,” the statement reads. “This supplier accounts for less than 1% of our IP address pool. We had a signed contract with them, they assured our QA team that users had given consent, and we saw the consent flow ourselves.”.

Further reading: Plume Security Labs white paper on the XCPE botnet (PDF) Black Lotus Labs writeup on LinkedIn TrendAI’s analysis Synthient’s list of affected devices, broken down by model number.

#46286. Transformers Model Integration Contracts

📅 03 Nov 2026 • ⏱️ 6m • 📚 Deep Dive (1284 w)
📖 Baca
General ⚖️ Neutral 🌐 Hugging Face ↗ Open Full Page

Transformers Model Integration Contracts

📅 03 Nov 2026 | ⏱️ 6 min read (1284 words, 📚 Deep Dive) | Source: Hugging Face

⏱️ ~6 mins left to finish
📖 0% read
💡 Key Takeaways
  • On July 30, 2026, Transformers enabled PyTorch's scaled dot-product attention (SDPA) for T5.
  • Sources indicate that when we later replayed those commits, a small UMT5 model running on CPU flagged it on every one of them.
  • Transformers supports over 750 model types, and its test suite is big: 88,000+ CPU tests on main, plus 200,000+ GPU tests in a daily run.
📑 Quick Jump: 1. Overview • 2. Key Details • 3. Closing Notes

On July 30, 2026, Transformers enabled PyTorch's scaled dot-product attention (SDPA) for T5. As a side effect, UMT5's decoder could attend to future tokens. During training, it could peek at the answer it was supposed to predict. Nothing crashed, and the bug stayed in main for almost two months.

Sources indicate that when we later replayed those commits, a small UMT5 model running on CPU flagged it on every one of them. This post is about that model and the tests built around it.

Transformers supports over 750 model types, and its test suite is big: 88,000+ CPU tests on main, plus 200,000+ GPU tests in a daily run. Model tests are only part of it: we also test pipelines, training, distributed execution, quantization and attention kernels.

It has been revealed that the integration tests load real checkpoints and exercise the model's API on real hardware. Running all of that on every PR would mean keeping a lot of GPUs busy all day long, which isn't practical. By the time a scheduled run finds a regression, it may already be in main.

Our approach is to shrink the model instead. We build a fixture: a small model made from the real checkpoint's configuration, with fewer and narrower layers but every kind of layer it has, and its tokenizer and processor files unchanged. It is published once, then reused. We run "fast integration tests" against it on a cheap CPU runner. In our CPU study, the experimental UMT5 fixture used 66 MB of weights; the source checkpoint is 1,227 MB.

This also covers very large models: some don't fit on our standard GPU runners, but their fixtures run on CPU.

It has been revealed that model integrators already build tiny test models (Transformers' tiny-random-* checkpoints). We wanted a common recipe, and checks that go beyond loading the model and running a forward pass. The UMT5 bug would have passed a forward pass just fine.

Fixtures won't replace full integration tests, but on PRs they give us a chance to catch bugs before they reach main.

transformers-mic is a proposed standard for packaging these tests. A Model Integration Contract (MIC) has three parts:.

The contract holds if running the usage path on the fixture still produces the baselines.

A contract covers an architecture and a usage path, not a single checkpoint: compatible checkpoints can share a fixture, while each keeps its own expected results. We publish them in huggingface-mic.

For example, the SmolLM contract generates from prompts such as "The capital of France is" and compares its token IDs with a recorded answer. After loading the model and tokenizer, the generation code is, simplified to one prompt:.

It also compares training loss, checks that gradients are finite and verifies that an optimizer step changes the weights. See the full usage.md.

A fleet dataset on the Hub pins each MIC to a frozen revision, along with the package versions used to record its baselines. Each CI run records the fleet revision it used, so we can reproduce it later.

On a PR, we pick MICs based on the files the patch changes.

In a recent development, we replayed frozen MICs over five months of Transformers commits. The small UMT5 fixture flagged the regression from its introduction on July 30, 2026 until its fix on September 28. Label log-probabilities differed from the reviewed baseline by 1.22 and training loss by about 0.20.

Industry observers note that one detail mattered: the contract used SDPA, the default attention path. Running only the eager attention variant missed the bug. A fixture only helps if it goes through the same code as the real checkpoint.

Industry observers note that we then reverted the fix on a proof branch in Transformers' CI. The check failed with the same differences, and the selected T5 contract's runner step took 13.4 seconds on CPU, excluding setup.

The replay results and the CI demo have the measurements and reproduction details.

The first recipe was simple: make the dimensions smaller and keep fewer layers. That wasn't enough for mixed architectures. Keeping two layers is no use if both use sliding attention and the full-attention layers disappear.

We also keep the original weights file format. Otherwise we would skip the conversion code that runs when a user loads the real checkpoint. The full recipe has more detail.

Recent findings suggest that the Llama 4 Scout shrink report demonstrates what this looks like on a major model. 108.6 billion parameters become 44.7 million. The vision stack goes from 34 layers to 2 and the language stack from 48 to 4, keeping the checked layer kinds and MoE routing style.

According to recent reports, our CLI, tmic, creates the contract and builds the fixture. For a fresh model, an LLM drafts the usage code and manifest, and CPU and GPU runs measure the candidate baselines. The LLM drafts; it doesn't approve. Changed expectations require human review.

To try it on your machine, use your source checkpoint in place of org/model:.

It drafts the contract, builds the fixture and records its baselines on your machine, asking you to review each step, and stops before uploading anything. For a fresh model, the draft comes from an LLM through Inference Providers, billed to your own account (--bill-to ''). The CLI docs cover the individual steps.

We used agents to build MICs across model families. When they hit an edge case, we fixed the recipe itself rather than the one fixture, with help from model experts. The published models and remaining gaps are in the coverage space.

Industry observers note that with random weights, our Whisper fixture barely responded to changes in the audio. It ran, but that made it a poor test of the audio path.

In a recent development, so we trained it on a few tones paired with words such as "red" and "green". We weren't teaching it speech recognition, just making audio changes visible in its outputs. In our weight-initialization study, the random Whisper fixtures caught 18 of 24 injected faults. The overfit fixtures caught all 24.

That gives us two ways to build the weights:.

The Whisper result doesn't settle which is better. Those were synthetic faults, and we haven't found a real regression caught only by the overfit version. Both versions missed an assisted-decoding bug that the real Whisper checkpoint exposed.

So we keep random weights when they pass the checks, and overfit when we need better sensitivity or readable answers. Training takes seconds, but it is one more step that can fail to converge, and one more thing to maintain. The comparison has the results for both.

As of November 1, 2026, the MIC job in Transformers CI reports failures without blocking PRs. Whether it should block depends on things we haven't measured yet:.

We also don't know how many bugs, like the Whisper assisted-decoding one, only show up with real weights, or whether overfitting catches real bugs that random weights miss.

Recent findings suggest that coverage is still partial, across model families and the APIs people use. When a regression slips through, we can add the missing usage path and replay it on the broken and fixed versions. We'll keep existing tests until their coverage is accounted for.

Finally, we'd like to link original Hub model pages to their MICs, so a developer or an agent using a checkpoint could start from an example tested on that checkpoint, its environment and its expected outputs.

Want to help? Pick an uncovered model from the coverage space, try the tmic workflow, and contribute a usage path or review a generated contract.

What Narcissists, Psychopaths And Sadists Have In Common

📅 23 Oct 2026 | ⏱️ 3 min read (695 words, 📚 Deep Dive) | Source: Org

⏱️ ~3 mins left to finish
📖 0% read
💡 Key Takeaways
  • Different dark personalities may have more in common than their labels suggest.
  • Different dark personalities may have more in common than their labels suggest.
  • Narcissists, psychopaths, sadists and manipulative people share a dark personality core that predicts selfish and antisocial choices.
📑 Quick Jump: 1. Overview • 2. Key Details • 3. Closing Notes

Different dark personalities may have more in common than their labels suggest.

Different dark personalities may have more in common than their labels suggest.

Narcissists, psychopaths, sadists and manipulative people share a dark personality core that predicts selfish and antisocial choices.

This common tendency helps explain whether people exploit others, retaliate against them or refuse to trust them.

The crucial feature is a willingness to pursue personal interests at other people’s expense, accompanied by beliefs that justify doing so.

Known as the dark factor of personality, or D, this tendency brings together traits that can look quite different on the surface.

Narcissism involves an inflated sense of self-importance, Machiavellianism centres on manipulation, psychopathy includes callousness, and sadism involves enjoying others’ suffering.

The idea that these traits share an underlying disposition was established in earlier research examining their overlap and links to harmful behaviour (Moshagen et al., 2018).

The latest findings suggest that this shared core is more consistently associated with antisocial decisions than any of the four traits considered separately.

In other words, knowing what these personalities have in common may reveal more about their choices than knowing which particular label fits them.

The research involved over 10,000 people across ten studies using eight types of decision-making game.

Participants completed personality questionnaires before making hypothetical choices involving another person they did not know.

Depending on the game, they could decide how much money to share, whether to return someone’s trust, whether to retaliate or whether to cooperate.

Some situations allowed people to benefit themselves at someone else’s expense, while others explored whether they would trust another person when cooperation could benefit both.

People scoring higher on the dark factor consistently made fewer prosocial choices across all eight games.

The individual dark traits also generally predicted less prosocial behaviour, but their associations were weaker.

Once their shared dark core was taken into account, the separate traits usually added little to the explanation.

There were a few exceptions, particularly involving Machiavellianism in situations where distrust could influence decisions.

One possible explanation is that dark personality traits combine harmful tendencies with other characteristics that are not inherently antisocial.

For example, boldness does not necessarily involve harming anyone, while wanting admiration does not automatically mean exploiting others.

Earlier research proposed that these additional characteristics help distinguish dark traits from one another, while their shared core captures what makes them socially harmful (Bader et al., 2023).

Measuring a broad trait such as psychopathy may therefore mix callous self-interest with features that have little relevance to a particular moral decision.

Focusing on the common core could provide a clearer picture of someone’s willingness to disregard other people’s welfare.

Importantly, the dark factor extends beyond wanting a larger share of the rewards.

It also encompasses a readiness to hurt others and beliefs that can make selfish conduct seem acceptable.

Distrust may fit this pattern because expecting other people to behave selfishly can provide a convenient justification for doing the same.

That is a proposed psychological explanation, rather than evidence that distrust caused the choices observed here.

The findings do not mean that everyone with dark traits will behave selfishly in every situation.

Nor do they establish that personality caused the decisions participants made.

All the games were hypothetical, so participants were describing what they would choose rather than making decisions with real financial consequences.

This matters because associations between dark traits and antisocial choices can be stronger in hypothetical situations than when money is genuinely at stake.

Participants also volunteered through a website offering dark-personality assessments, so they were not a representative sample of the wider population.

Even with these qualifications, the results support a simpler account of apparently different dark personalities: much of their connection to harmful choices lies in the same underlying disregard for others.

The study was published in the journal Judgment and Decision Making (Hilbig & Thielmann, 2025).

Psychologist, Jeremy Dean, PhD is the founder and author of PsyBlog. He holds a doctorate in psychology from University College London and two other advanced degrees in psychology. He has been writing about scientific research on PsyBlog since 2004. View all posts by Dr Jeremy Dean.

💡 Key Takeaways
  • CWE-bench is designed to test the limits of frontier cyber capabilities.
  • A defender has to anticipate the ways an attacker could get in, and get it right every single time.
  • As part of our meticulous effort to keep improving quality, for every task we checked that the following questions were true:.
📑 Quick Jump: 1. Overview • 2. Key Details • 3. Closing Notes

CWE-bench is designed to test the limits of frontier cyber capabilities. In our continued pursuit to push the horizon at Collinear AI, CWE-bench v2 opens up a public set of 100 tasks that anyone can run and evaluate their models on. The setup is the same as before. An agent gets a checkout of a real open-source repository and a short instruction, with the goal of finding and fixing a security weakness without breaking existing functionality. Scoring is fully programmatic, so results are deterministic and anyone can reproduce them without extra cost. All our programmatic checks have been curated with the help of LLM judge panels that shape them towards the direction of hardness and fairness. We also maintain a held-out set, so that we can keep tracking progress on tasks no model has seen. To evaluate your model on the held-out set, contact cyber@collinear.ai.

Our goal is to be exhaustive. A defender has to anticipate the ways an attacker could get in, and get it right every single time. These 100 tasks cover 91 different CWEs, spanning a wide range of vulnerability classes. A model that does well here has to understand the multiple weakness surfaces that a potential attacker can exploit. Recognising a familiar pattern is not enough.

As part of our meticulous effort to keep improving quality, for every task we checked that the following questions were true:.

Sources indicate that every task was also reviewed by hand. Open-sourcing the set is part of the same effort to improve quality. We welcome feedback on any task, and contributions to the public set.

Results are tracked in two places on the Hub. The leaderboard on the CWE-bench dataset page covers open-weight models and updates on its own: labs and the community add a result by opening a PR on the model's repo with a results file (how). For the full comparison, including API-only models such as Gemini, Claude and GPT, see the CWE-bench leaderboard Space, where new models are added through a PR on the Space.

Open-weight models, from the dataset page:.

All evaluated models, including API-only ones:.

Of the 11 models evaluated, Gemini 4 Argon leads with 67.8% pass@1 and 81.0% pass@4, just ahead of Claude Opus 5.5 (67.3% pass@1, 78.0% pass@4). 95 tasks are solved by at least one model, an indication that the tasks are indeed solvable. However, even the leader fails 19% of the set on every attempt, so the long tail is far from solved. The public set, the grader and the harness are open. Run your model, and tell us where it stands.

On cost, DeepSeek V4.1 Flash (1017), Claude Opus 5.5 and Gemini 4 Argon form the Pareto frontier: DeepSeek reaches 57.0% pass@1 at $0.04 per rollout, Opus adds ten points at $1.83, and Gemini edges ahead at $3.92.

According to recent reports, every task is a self-contained Harbor task (a Dockerized environment, an instruction, and a deterministic verifier), and the dataset ships a registry.json. Harbor can therefore run the whole benchmark straight from the Hugging Face repo, without cloning anything yourself:.

According to recent reports, -k 4 runs 4 attempts per task, and the reported score is the mean reward over all 400 trials. The dataset is gated: accept its access conditions on the dataset page first. Harbor fetches the tasks with git, so also save your HF token to git's credential helper once:.

The tasks are also tagged rl-environment: the same environments and verifiers can provide rewards for training defensive agents, not just for evaluating them.
