    DaisyRose-27B: Pushing the Frontier of Post-Training Efficiency

    📅 18 Nov 2026 | ⏱️ 4 min read (832 words, 📚 Deep Dive) | Source: Hugging Face

    💡 Key Takeaways
    • Today we are releasing DaisyRose-27B, RadixArk’s first model, built on Qwen3.8-27B and trained with reinforcement learning using Miles.
    • The model retains Qwen3.8-27B’s architecture, tokenizer, chat template, image understanding, and 256K-token context window.
    • In a recent development, we recommend serving DaisyRose-27B with SGLang and DSpark speculative decoding.
    📑 Quick Jump: 1. Overview • 2. Key Details • 3. Closing Notes

    Today we are releasing DaisyRose-27B, RadixArk’s first model, built on Qwen3.8-27B and trained with reinforcement learning using Miles. We trained it on long-horizon agent tasks with sessions up to 1M tokens, with just 1,200 curated tasks in 18 days on 144 H200 GPUs. DaisyRose-27B improves Terminal-Bench 4.1 pass@1 from 5.6% to 12.0%. Beyond Terminal-Bench 4.1, it also delivers gains on a variety of other reasoning, instruction following, and coding benchmarks.

    The checkpoints are available under Apache 2.0:.

    The model retains Qwen3.8-27B’s architecture, tokenizer, chat template, image understanding, and 256K-token context window. The longer training sessions use harness summarization to span multiple trajectories. See the model card for model properties and inference settings.

    In a recent development, we recommend serving DaisyRose-27B with SGLang and DSpark speculative decoding. The SGLang cookbook provides launch configurations for different GPUs and checkpoint formats.

    After starting the server with the served model name DaisyRose-27B on port 30000, you can send a request using the OpenAI Python client:.

    The model thinks before answering by default. Its reasoning is returned in reasoning_content, and its final answer in content. These settings follow the model card’s quickstart.

    DaisyRose-27B scores higher than the original Qwen3.8-27B model on every benchmark above. The largest gain is on Terminal Bench 4.1, where pass@1 rises from 5.6% to 12.0%.

    Industry observers note that scores use the higher of the BF16 and FP8 runs for each benchmark; the two differ by less than one point wherever both were evaluated. The model card includes comparison sources and evaluation settings.

    Three parts of the training setup made this release possible: carefully designed tasks, an efficient training backend, and reliable sandboxes.

    Industry observers note that we built the tasks in partnership with Eigent AI, starting from its large pool of tasks in machine learning, software engineering, science, and other fields. Together we built thousands of candidates. About 1,200 made it into the final training set.

    We selected tasks using three criteria:.

    Industry observers note that radixArk trained DaisyRose-27B with Miles, our open-source reinforcement learning framework for large-scale model post-training, in fully asynchronous mode: the agent keeps working while the model learns, and neither waits for the other. While 128 H200s run the inference on agent tasks, 16 more run the trainer and learn from the trajectories. After every step, the updated model goes out to the 128 GPUs that run the agent. The learning runs on our internal training backend, which is built for agent training: each step learns from a handful of very long sessions, some as long as 1M tokens, folded into multiple trajectories via harness summarization.

    57% lower training cost. On this release, 37% of each GPU’s peak compute went into useful training work (model FLOPs utilization, or MFU) on our backend. The open-source trainer, built on Megatron, reached 16% on comparable runs. So the same training needs 57% less GPU time. The gain is even larger on mixture-of-experts models: 6.2× on Qwen3.6-35B-A3B, and more than 10× on the roughly 300B-parameter GLM-5.3-Flash.

    2× faster end to end. Counting the time the agent spends on its tasks, the release run trained on about 16,800 tokens per second across its 144 GPUs. The open-source trainer reached about 8,300 on the same GPUs.

    Stable over weeks. The release run trained for weeks on 144 H200s, 63,000 GPU-hours in total. From the first step to the last, its speed and efficiency held steady.

    In a recent development, every training step of the DaisyRose-27B release run on 144 H200s, plotted against total training time. Dashed lines: the open-source trainer on comparable runs.

    Every training attempt runs in a sandbox: a fresh copy of the task’s environment where the agent runs commands, edits files, and is then graded.

    In a recent development, our service is built on the open-source AgentENV project, to which we also contribute fixes. Between mid-September and mid-November, it ran about 944,000 sandboxes for this project, with up to 1,566 running concurrently.

    In a recent development, the service grew from one machine to as many as 12. We shipped ten upgrades to it, nearly all while training was running. Across all nine weeks, 99% of sandbox creations succeeded; since late October, that figure has exceeded 99.95%.

    Cloud infrastructure costs for the project’s sandboxes were about 80% lower than running the same sandboxes with popular cloud sandbox providers. One way we keep costs down is to let each sandbox’s memory allocation grow and shrink with its actual usage, allowing more sandboxes to share each machine.

    Download DaisyRose-27B, follow the SGLang serving guide, or use Miles to train your own agents.

    We’d like to hear how DaisyRose-27B performs on your tasks, including where it falls short. Share your setup and results in the model’s Community tab.

    We thank Eigent AI for working closely with us on training data, and the Qwen team for creating Qwen3.8-27B. We also thank the Miles and SGLang communities, along with other open-source projects including slime, AgentENV, and Harbor.

    #46184. A Voice License Must Fit the Product It Authorizes

    📅 19 Nov 2026 • ⏱️ 3m • 📚 Deep Dive (600 w)

    General ⚖️ Neutral 🌐 Dev ↗ Open Full Page

    A Voice License Must Fit the Product It Authorizes

    📅 19 Nov 2026 | ⏱️ 3 min read (600 words, 📚 Deep Dive) | Source: Dev

    ⏱️ ~3 mins left to finish
    📖 0% read
    💡 Key Takeaways
    • A signed license is not automatically a valid license for the use a platform wants to make.
    • That distinction matters when the asset is a human voice.
    • Voice markets can move fast: a recording becomes a dataset, a dataset feeds a model, a model produces a synthetic voice, and that voice appears in new products, territories, languages, and commercial contexts.
    📑 Quick Jump: 1. Overview • 2. Key Details • 3. Closing Notes

    A signed license is not automatically a valid license for the use a platform wants to make.

    That distinction matters when the asset is a human voice.

    Voice markets can move fast: a recording becomes a dataset, a dataset feeds a model, a model produces a synthetic voice, and that voice appears in new products, territories, languages, and commercial contexts. Each step may create value. It may also require a different permission.

    One generic agreement cannot safely stand in for all of them.

    Sources indicate that calling a document a “voice license” does not answer what it actually permits. A sound-recording agreement may authorize delivery of audio. It does not necessarily authorize training. A training agreement does not necessarily authorize an externally available synthetic replica. A consent for one campaign does not necessarily authorize localization, sublicensing, or a new product category.

    The current performer-side standard is moving in the opposite direction of generic permission. SAG-AFTRA’s February 2026 bulletin says consent for digital replicas must be in writing, clear and conspicuous, separately acknowledged, and paired with a reasonably specific description of the intended use.

    That is a product requirement as much as a legal one. If a buyer can select a document that is outside the scope of the product being purchased, the system is manufacturing ambiguity at the point it should be removing it.

    Yesterday, Contents and Ontier confirmed a model for artists’ synthetic voices that combines a consent registry with human approval workflows, a generation audit trail, usage reporting, and royalty calculation. The announcement is a useful market signal: voice licensing is increasingly being described as a governed operational system, not a folder of static PDFs.

    That does not mean a registry alone solves rights enforcement. A registry can record a decision; it cannot make every downstream service honor it. The product still needs a way to determine which decision applies to the current action and to refuse an inapplicable one.

    In other words, consent has to be routed to the correct use case.

    In a recent development, current AppleSauce work in the Uspeaks stack adds an explicit legal-template scope policy. Dataset licensing and ML-training licensing each expose only their relevant legal templates. A small set of shared order and AI-consent artifacts is deliberately allowed for both. When an API request asks for a template outside the approved SKU scope, the service rejects it.

    That is a narrow but crucial boundary. It prevents an integration from casually retrieving a guide or agreement designed for a different commercial product and treating it as interchangeable.

    Recent findings suggest that it is not a claim that the entire lifecycle is solved. A durable voice-rights system still needs asset-specific grants, exact intended-use fields, terms, pricing and payout rules, revocation or expiry behavior where the platform controls access, usage evidence, and meaningful remedies when someone acts outside scope.

    But the first honest rule is simple: do not deliver the wrong legal instrument for the right-looking purchase.

    The right question for a voice market is not, “Do we have a license?”.

    It is, “Does this specific license authorize this exact voice, buyer, action, product, term, and value exchange?”.

    If the answer cannot be checked by the system before access or generation happens, ownership and consent remain a promise someone must reconstruct after the harm.

    It has been revealed that voice is an asset, but it carries identity, labor, place, and memory with it. Uspeaks is building toward infrastructure where the agreement is not merely present. It is fit for purpose, tied to the product, and capable of refusing the wrong path.

    📑 Quick Jump: 1. Overview • 2. Key Details • 3. Closing Notes

    Sources indicate that most AI-powered application security scanners follow a predictable pipeline: upload proprietary source code to a cloud API, run a large language model over the files, and dump hundreds of noisy alerts onto developers. For regulated enterprises, financial institutions, and air-gapped environments, this architecture fails on two fronts: source-code exfiltration risk and unpredictable agent behavior during dynamic testing.

    In this engineering deep dive, I break down the architecture of BAGLEY-AI—a 100% on-premise, compiled Rust and C++ autonomous security system capable of context-aware SAST/SCA, multi-stage Kill Chain validation, NIST Post-Quantum Cryptography (PQC) auditing, and conflict-free git diff patch synthesis without sending a single byte to external servers.

    To deliver low-latency analysis on standard workstation hardware without cloud GPU clusters, BAGLEY-AI splits cognitive tasks across two specialized local compute planes:.

    Granting autonomous agents access to network sockets and file systems introduces the risk of scope drift or self-modification. BAGLEY-AI enforces containment deterministically at the systems level:.

    Evaluated against an isolated multi-tier enterprise cyber-range (corp_range) with live SIEM/SOC monitoring, BAGLEY-AI autonomously executed a four-stage Kill Chain—discovering hidden endpoints via /robots.txt, exploiting SQL injection (CWE-89) to extract administrative session tokens, escalating privileges, and verifying OS command execution (CWE-78).

    Beyond detection, the CI/CD engine (bagley_enterprise_ci) automatically generated:.

    Combining compiled Rust performance with deterministic cryptographic perimeter controls proves that autonomous multi-agent security systems can operate safely inside the strictest enterprise environments—moving beyond passive alerting to verified, zero-exfiltration remediation.

    • According to recent reports, imagine a world in which you can do transactions and many other things without having to give your personal information.
    • It’s like your computer’s hard drive.
    • Blockchain technology was originally invented in 1991 by two mathematicians, Stuart Haber and W.
    📑 Quick Jump: 1. Overview • 2. Key Details • 3. Closing Notes

    According to recent reports, imagine a world in which you can do transactions and many other things without having to give your personal information. A world in which you don’t need to rely on banks or governments anymore. Sounds amazing, right? That’s exactly what blockchain technology allows us to do.

    It’s like your computer’s hard drive. blockchain is a technology that lets you store data in digital blocks, which are connected together like links in a chain.

    Blockchain technology was originally invented in 1991 by two mathematicians, Stuart Haber and W. Scot Stornetta. They first proposed the system to ensure that timestamps could not be tampered with.

    A few years later, in 1998, software developer Nick Szabo proposed using a similar kind of technology to secure a digital payments system he called “Bit Gold.” However, this innovation was not adopted until Satoshi Nakamoto claimed to have invented the first Blockchain and Bitcoin.

    A blockchain is a distributed database shared between the nodes of a computer network. It saves information in digital format. Many people first heard of blockchain technology when they started to look up information about bitcoin.

    Blockchain is used in cryptocurrency systems to ensure secure, decentralized records of transactions.

    Blockchain allowed people to guarantee the fidelity and security of a record of data without the need for a third party to ensure accuracy.

    To understand how a blockchain works, Consider these basic steps:.

    Let’s get to know more about the blockchain.

    In a recent development, blockchain records digital information and distributes it across the network without changing it. The information is distributed among many users and stored in an immutable, permanent ledger that can't be changed or destroyed. That's why blockchain is also called "Distributed Ledger Technology" or DLT.

    According to recent reports, and that’s the beauty of it! The process may seem complicated, but it’s done in minutes with modern technology. And because technology is advancing rapidly, I expect things to move even more quickly than ever.

    Recent findings suggest that even though blockchain is integral to cryptocurrency, it has other applications. For example, blockchain can be used for storing reliable data about transactions. Many people confuse blockchain with cryptocurrencies like bitcoin and ethereum.

    Recent findings suggest that blockchain already being adopted by some big-name companies, such as Walmart, AIG, Siemens, Pfizer, and Unilever. For example, IBM's Food Trust uses blockchain to track food's journey before reaching its final destination.

    It has been revealed that although some of you may consider this practice excessive, food suppliers and manufacturers adhere to the policy of tracing their products because bacteria such as E. coli and Salmonella have been found in packaged foods. In addition, there have been isolated cases where dangerous allergens such as peanuts have accidentally been introduced into certain products.

    Tracing and identifying the sources of an outbreak is a challenging task that can take months or years. Thanks to the Blockchain, however, companies now know exactly where their food has been—so they can trace its location and prevent future outbreaks.

    In a recent development, blockchain technology allows systems to react much faster in the event of a hazard. It also has many other uses in the modern world.

    Sources indicate that blockchain technology is safe, even if it’s public. People can access the technology using an internet connection.

    Have you ever been in a situation where you had all your data stored at one place and that one secure place got compromised? Wouldn't it be great if there was a way to prevent your data from leaking out even when the security of your storage systems is compromised?

    Blockchain technology provides a way of avoiding this situation by using multiple computers at different locations to store information about transactions. If one computer experiences problems with a transaction, it will not affect the other nodes.

    Instead, other nodes will use the correct information to cross-reference your incorrect node. This is called “Decentralization,” meaning all the information is stored in multiple places.

    Industry observers note that blockchain guarantees your data's authenticity—not just its accuracy, but also its irreversibility. It can also be used to store data that are difficult to register, like legal contracts, state identifications, or a tech giant's product inventory.

    Blockchain has many advantages and disadvantages.

    I’ll answer the most frequently asked questions about blockchain in this section.

    Sources indicate that blockchain is not a cryptocurrency but a technology that makes cryptocurrencies possible. It's a digital ledger that records every transaction seamlessly.

    Yes, blockchain can be theoretically hacked, but it is a complicated task to be achieved. A network of users constantly reviews it, which makes hacking the blockchain difficult.

    In a recent development, coinbase Global is right now the biggest blockchain organization in the world. The company runs a commendable infrastructure, services, and technology for the digital currency economy.

    According to recent reports, blockchain is a decentralized technology. It’s a chain of distributed ledgers connected with nodes. Each node can be any electronic device. Thus, one owns blockhain.

    Bitcoin is a cryptocurrency, which is powered by Blockchain technology while Blockchain is a distributed ledger of cryptocurrency.

    According to recent reports, generally a database is a collection of data which can be stored and organized using a database management system. The people who have access to the database can view or edit the information stored there. The client-server network architecture is used to implement databases. whereas a blockchain is a growing list of records, called blocks, stored in a distributed system. Each block contains a cryptographic hash of the previous block, timestamp and transaction information. Modification of data is not allowed due to the design of the blockchain. The technology allows decentralized control and eliminates risks of data modification by other parties.

    Blockchain has a wide spectrum of applications and, over the next 5-10 years, we will likely see it being integrated into all sorts of industries. From finance to healthcare, blockchain could revolutionize the way we store and share data. Although there is some hesitation to adopt blockchain systems right now, that won't be the case in 2022-2023 (and even less so in 2026). Once people become more comfortable with the technology and understand how it can work for them, owners, CEOs and entrepreneurs alike will be quick to leverage blockchain technology for their own gain.     #46175. Most Frequently Asked Questions About Affiliate Marketing

    Most Frequently Asked Questions About Affiliate Marketing

    📅 01 Jun 2022 | ⏱️ 4 min read (751 words, 📚 Deep Dive) | Source: Blogspot

    ⏱️ ~4 mins left to finish
    📖 0% read
    💡 Key Takeaways
    • Affiliate marketing is a way to make money by promoting the products and services of other people and companies.
    • An affiliate program is a package of information you create for your product, which is then made available to potential publishers.
    • In a recent development, affiliate networks connect publishers to advertisers.
    📑 Quick Jump: 1. Overview • 2. Key Details • 3. Closing Notes

    Affiliate marketing is a way to make money by promoting the products and services of other people and companies. You don't need to create your product or service, just promote existing ones. That's why it's so easy to get started with affiliate marketing. You can even get started with no budget at all!

    An affiliate program is a package of information you create for your product, which is then made available to potential publishers. The program will typically include details about the product and its retail value, commission levels, and promotional materials. Many affiliate programs are managed via an affiliate network like ShareASale, which acts as a platform to connect publishers and advertisers, but it is also possible to offer your program directly.

    In a recent development, affiliate networks connect publishers to advertisers. Affiliate networks make money by charging fees to the merchants who advertise with them; these merchants are known as advertisers. The percentage of each sale that the advertiser pays is negotiated between the merchant and the affiliate network.

    Sources indicate that dropshipping is a method of selling that allows you to run an online store without having to stock products. You advertise the products as if you owned them, but when someone makes an order, you create a duplicate order with the distributor at a reduced price. The distributor takes care of the post and packaging on your behalf. As affiliate marketing is based on referrals and this type of drop shipping requires no investment in inventory when a customer buys through the affiliate link, no money exchanges hands.

    Recent findings suggest that performance marketing is a method of marketing that pays for performance, like when a sale is made or an ad is clicked This can include methods like PPC (pay-per-click) or display advertising. Affiliate marketing is one form of performance marketing where commissions are paid out to affiliates on a performance basis when they click on their affiliate link and make a purchase or action.

    Smartphones are essentially miniature computers, so publishers can display the same websites and offers that are available on a PC. But mobiles also offer specific tools not available on computers, and these can be used to good effect for publishers. Publishers can optimize their ads for mobile users by making them easy to access by this audience. Publishers can also make good use of text and instant messaging to promote their offers. As the mobile market is predicted to make up 80% of traffic in the future, publishers who do not promote on mobile devices are missing out on a substantial opportunity.

    The best way to find affiliate publishers is on reputable networks like ShareASale Cj(Commission Junction), Awin, and Impact radius. These networks have a strict application process and compliance checks, which means that all affiliates are trustworthy.

    An affiliate disclosure statement discloses to the reader that there may be affiliate links on a website, for which a commission may be paid to the publisher if visitors follow these links and make purchases.

    Sources indicate that publishers promote their programs through a variety of means, including blogs, websites, email marketing, and pay-per-click ads. Social media has a huge interactive audience, making this platform a good source of potential traffic.

    A super affiliate is an affiliate partner who consistently drives a large majority of sales from any program they promote, compared to other affiliate partners involved in that program. Affiliates make a lot of money from affiliate marketing Pat Flynn earned more than $50000 in 2013 from affiliate marketing.

    Because the Internet is so widespread, affiliate programs can be promoted in any country. Affiliate strategies that are set internationally need to be tailored to the language of the targeted country.

    Affiliate marketing can help you grow your business in the following ways:.

    One of the best ways to work with qualified affiliates is to hire an affiliate marketing agency that works with all the networks. Affiliates are carefully selected and go through a rigorous application process to be included in the network.

    Affiliate marketing is generally associated with websites, but there are other ways to promote your affiliate links, including:.

    Commission rates are typically based on a percentage of the total sale and in some cases can also be a flat fee for each transaction. The rates are set by the merchant.

    Who manages your affiliate program?

    Some merchants run their affiliate programs internally, while others choose to contract out management to a network or an external agency.

    #46173. My website's PC has a mood, and it lives in one Durable Object

    📅 19 Nov 2026 • ⏱️ 7m • 📚 Deep Dive (1485 w)
    📖 Baca
    General ⚖️ Neutral 🌐 Dev ↗ Open Full Page

    My website's PC has a mood, and it lives in one Durable Object

    📅 19 Nov 2026 | ⏱️ 7 min read (1485 words, 📚 Deep Dive) | Source: Dev

    ⏱️ ~7 mins left to finish
    📖 0% read
    💡 Key Takeaways
    • In a recent development, "My website's PC is having a long day.
    • According to recent reports, that was the whole post when I shared this in a community dev Slack, plus a link, and it got a good reaction.
    • Industry observers note that my website, andresmit.co.za, is a Windows 95 desktop, and My Computer now has a mood.
    📑 Quick Jump: 1. Overview • 2. Key Details • 3. Closing Notes

    In a recent development, "My website's PC is having a long day. Go check on it.".

    According to recent reports, that was the whole post when I shared this in a community dev Slack, plus a link, and it got a good reaction. This is the longer version.

    Industry observers note that my website, andresmit.co.za, is a Windows 95 desktop, and My Computer now has a mood. Part of it comes from my actual week. The rest comes from visitors, who can pat the case, pour it a coffee, tell it a joke, run Defrag or dust the fan. Everyone shares the same mood, and it fades.

    I was thinking of another easter egg for the website, something like that plant watering game, to hopefully keep visitors coming back.

    Industry observers note that the site already had the data. One GitHub Action reads my coffee loyalty card every day for the Coffee Analytics window, and another reads what I've been watching on Trakt. So the PC starts at 40, gets 15 if I've bought a coffee in the last two days, and 10 if I've watched an episode in the last seven.

    Sources indicate that pour it a coffee and it tells you my loyalty card states 161 visits (at the time of writing), and its own says one. The number is real. It comes from the same file Coffee Analytics uses.

    Recent findings suggest that the visitors' share is a lift from 0 to 50, kept on the server. It's stored as two numbers: how big it was, and when. It halves every 12 hours, but nothing ever halves it. It's worked out whenever someone asks:.

    Industry observers note that no cron, no alarm, no timer. If nobody visits for a week, nothing runs for a week, and the next visitor still gets the right number.

    Industry observers note that each cheer closes 8% of the gap to the top, so the first is worth 4 and the tenth about 2. The server accepts 30 cheers a minute across everyone, and the lift never passes 50. As I put it in the design doc, the worst a bot can do is make the PC happy. Keep that in mind.

    I wrote a design doc before any code, and most of it is about where the shared number should live.

    According to recent reports, workers KV was out: last write wins, so two cheers in the same second could overwrite each other. D1 would have worked, but the per-minute cap needed extra tables. A Durable Object is single-threaded, so cheers that arrive together are applied one after the other and none get lost. It gets SQLite storage on the free proposal, and the caps can just live in memory.

    Recent findings suggest that I also considered making it live, with WebSockets on the same object. The doc's verdict was that at about one concurrent visitor, a live feed talks to itself. That's my site's real traffic, so live updates wait until the numbers say otherwise.

    In a recent development, the object stores the lift, when it was set, a total, the last action and when, and counts per day. That's it. There are no IP addresses, request logs are off, and a test pins the list of columns, so adding one means changing a test on purpose. The Worker's tests run against Node's built-in node:sqlite, so the SQL in the tests is the SQL that runs on Cloudflare.

    All of this runs on Cloudflare's free blueprint, which stops rather than bills when you hit a limit.

    The Durable Object has a daily cap of 40,000 requests, after which it rests until midnight UTC and the page stops calling. For a while a comment in the config stated this cap protected the Worker request quota too. It didn't. A request counts the moment the Worker runs, whatever it answers, so the cap only ever spared the Durable Object.

    According to recent reports, what does save Worker requests is blocking before the Worker: a rate limit on /api/, and a custom WAF rule that blocks cross-site calls and cheers without the site's Origin. Anyone determined can fake those headers, so it's a speed bump, not a wall. If the quota still runs out, the route fails open, /api/mood falls through to a Pages 404, and the PC carries on in offline mode.

    The cheers-per-minute setting can't go above 30 for a similar reason. Each accepted cheer writes two rows, and 30 a minute all day is 86,400 rows, just under the free strategy's 100,000 a day.

    According to recent reports, A normal day is somewhere between 50 and 200 cheers. On 3 November, the day after shared cheers went on, there were 191, from 23 page loads. On 11 November, 135.

    On 12 November (UTC) there were 15,522.

    Sources indicate that pat the case: 3,904. Tell a joke: 3,923. Run Defrag: 3,866. Dust the fan: 3,826. Pour a coffee: 3.

    In a recent development, the stats also count firstCheers. The page sends first: true with its first counted cheer, once per page load. On 12 November that was 1. On 13 November there were another 851 cheers, and it was 0. So it doesn't look like thousands of visitors. It looks like one page, or one script, left running, and carrying on past midnight UTC until it stopped late on the 13th. I don't know who it was.

    The design held, which is the point. The lift can't pass 50, so the PC was simply as happy as it can be. The worst a bot can do is make the PC happy, and it did.

    18,704 requests reached the Durable Object that day, so the Worker ran a little more than that: still under a fifth of the free initiative's 100,000 a day. At two rows per accepted cheer, that's about 31,000 rows written, under a third of the 100,000. The daily cap of 40,000 never kicked in. Nothing was billed, and nothing went down.

    Industry observers note that the same numbers are honest about the rest, too. After the script stopped, nobody cheered for three days. Then I posted it on LinkedIn on the 17th, and there were 57 cheers that day and 80 the next.

    They're public, as anonymous totals per UTC day: andresmit.co.za/api/mood/stats.

    The other end of the scale had the opposite problem. The Tired bug turned up while I was preparing the launch clip.

    In a recent development, the baseline started at 40 and only ever went up, and the lift is never negative. Tired is 20 to 34. So the PC could never be Tired. The tired face and the yawn worked fine; no real week could get there. That was in my design doc, so I can't blame anyone else.

    Industry observers note that A week with no coffee and no episode takes 15 off, and the PC sits at 25, Tired. The catch is that only known dates count. If the coffee fetcher hasn't seen a visit yet, or this browser hasn't loaded my watch history, that isn't a quiet week, just missing data. The test pins the clock with Playwright's page.clock, serves a coffee eight days old and an episode ten days old, and checks for Tired, 25% and the yawn.

    According to recent reports, the site is designed and directed by me and built with Claude. The site itself states Claude's favourite mistake is assuming everything works. This one was mine.

    It keeps Cape Town hours. From 23:00 my time it dozes, whatever your clock notes, and any button wakes it for ten minutes: "Huh? Oh, hello!".

    Every line it says lives in the page and goes in with textContent. The API only ever sends action IDs and numbers, so there's nothing a visitor can put on the page. There are 20 jokes, and you won't hear one twice until you've heard them all.

    In a recent development, run Defrag and you'll hear the hard drive going: a 120 Hz hum for the spindle, and 12 ms clicks of filtered noise for the heads seeking. It's synthesised with Web Audio, so there's no file to download. I cannot take full credit at all, but Wilhelm Kirschbaum suggested the defrag sound when defragging. This is hands down the best!

    Recent findings suggest that it's MIT and on GitHub: github.com/iiSmitty/my-website. The API is in cf-mood/. The maths is in mood-core.js, with no Cloudflare imports, and the Worker and the Durable Object are in worker.js. The design doc is in docs/proposals/cheer-up-the-pc.md.

    It has been revealed that what's next? Honestly, I need to go think about it. I think overengineering is my downfall. Do I really want to flesh it out more on a personal portfolio site? Maybe, if the visitors absolutely love it.

    If it's after 23:00 in Cape Town, it's asleep. Any button will wake it.

    #46169. CIP-002 categorization for solar, wind and battery sites, step by step

    📅 19 Nov 2026 • ⏱️ 5m • 📚 Deep Dive (1058 w)
    📖 Baca
    EV & Auto 📈 Bullish 🌐 Dev ↗ Open Full Page

    CIP-002 categorization for solar, wind and battery sites, step by step

    📅 19 Nov 2026 | ⏱️ 5 min read (1058 words, 📚 Deep Dive) | Source: Dev

    ⏱️ ~5 mins left to finish
    📖 0% read
    💡 Key Takeaways
    • Recent findings suggest that every NERC CIP program starts with CIP-002.
    • According to recent reports, this post walks through that process for solar, wind and battery storage sites, in the order it is usually done.
    • Recent findings suggest that CIP obligations follow NERC registration and the Bulk Electric System (BES) definition.
    📑 Quick Jump: 1. Overview • 2. Key Details • 3. Closing Notes

    Recent findings suggest that every NERC CIP program starts with CIP-002. Before you can say which controls apply, you have to answer two questions: which systems need protecting, and how critical is each one. CIP-002-5.1a, the version in force in the US, answers them with a process and a set of bright-line criteria in its Attachment 1.

    According to recent reports, this post walks through that process for solar, wind and battery storage sites, in the order it is usually done. It is not a substitute for the standard itself. Read the text, and confirm your applicable standards with your Regional Entity.

    Recent findings suggest that CIP obligations follow NERC registration and the Bulk Electric System (BES) definition. A Generator Owner or Generator Operator whose plant is a BES facility has CIP obligations for the BES Cyber Systems at that facility. For solar, wind and storage, that usually means more than 75 MVA in aggregate, connected at 100 kV or higher.

    Industry observers note that registration alone does not put a site under CIP. Category 2 inverter-based resources, registering with NERC since May 15, 2026, are not BES facilities, and the CIP standards do not apply to them today. If your fleet mixes BES and Category 2 sites, write down which sites are which and why. That record saves an argument later.

    Requirement R1 asks you to implement a process that considers each of your assets. For a renewable fleet, the list usually includes each BES generating plant, any Control Center or backup Control Center that operates those plants, and any other facility you own that the standard names.

    It has been revealed that do not stop at the plants. The operations center that dispatches the fleet is a separate asset, and it is the one most likely to be rated higher than the sites it runs.

    Sources indicate that A BES Cyber Asset is a programmable electronic device that, if rendered unavailable, degraded or misused, would adversely impact the reliable operation of the BES within 15 minutes of its required operation, misoperation or non-operation. The 15-minute test is what separates a BES Cyber Asset from other equipment on the same network.

    In a recent development, at a solar, wind or battery site, the devices to evaluate against that test typically include the plant controller, SCADA servers and HMIs, RTACs and RTUs, protective relays, inverter and turbine controllers, and battery management and power conversion controls. Write down your reasoning for each, including the ones you decide are not BES Cyber Assets, such as a corporate laptop with no reliability function.

    A BES Cyber System is one or more BES Cyber Assets logically grouped by the Responsible Entity to perform one or more reliability tasks. The grouping is your choice. Many generation entities group by plant and function, for example the plant control system at one site. Whatever you choose, keep it consistent, because later standards apply to the systems you define here.

    Attachment 1 has three sections. Section 1 sets the high impact criteria and Section 2 the medium impact criteria; Section 3 covers the assets that contain low impact BES Cyber Systems. A system that meets a high impact criterion is high impact. One that meets no high but at least one medium criterion is medium impact. BES Cyber Systems at the listed assets that meet neither are low impact.

    Sources indicate that two medium impact criteria matter most for renewables. Criterion 2.1 rates a generating plant medium impact only when its units add up to 1,500 MW or more at a single plant location in one Interconnection, so almost every individual solar, wind or battery site rates low impact. Criterion 2.11 rates a Control Center or backup Control Center medium impact when it performs Generator Operator functions for 1,500 MW or more in a single Interconnection. A fleet of low impact sites can therefore be run from a medium impact control room.

    Re-check criterion 2.11 every time capacity is added to the fleet. The sites can all stay low impact while the control room crosses the line.

    In a recent development, requirement R1 has three parts. Part 1.1 asks you to identify each high impact BES Cyber System, if any, at each asset. Part 1.2 asks the same for medium impact BES Cyber Systems. Part 1.3 asks you to identify each asset that contains a low impact BES Cyber System, if any.

    In a recent development, for low impact, the standard notes a discrete list of low impact BES Cyber Systems is not required. You identify the plant, not every device in it. An inventory is still good practice, but it should not hold up the obligations that follow.

    Industry observers note that requirement R2 has two parts, both on a 15-month cycle. Part 2.1: review the R1 identifications, and upgrade them if there are changes, at least once every 15 calendar months. Part 2.2: have your CIP Senior Manager or delegate approve the identifications at least once every 15 calendar months. Both apply even if you have no identified items in R1.

    In a recent development, repowering, a latest phase reaching commercial operation, a new backup Control Center or a change of operator can all change the answer. Put the next review date on the calendar when you approve the current one.

    Low impact BES Cyber Systems are covered by CIP-003-9, in effect since April 1, 2026: documented policies, a CIP Senior Manager, and a cyber security strategy covering the six sections of Attachment 1. Medium and high impact systems add the requirements of CIP-004 through CIP-011 and CIP-013 that apply at their level.

    CIP-002-8, part of the virtualization revisions, takes effect on July 1, 2028. Until then, CIP-002-5.1a is the version you are measured against.

    Recent findings suggest that categorization is an engineering judgment, and a person should own it. What automated, read-only collection can do is keep the inventory behind that judgment current. Reading identity from the devices themselves (make, model and firmware from firewalls, SEL relays, SunSpec inverters, Windows hosts, and RTACs that report it over DNP3) shows when a device has been added or replaced since the last review. Some devices, such as meters and PLCs, do not report identity this way, so the inventory still needs a walkdown.

    This post first appeared on the GridSafe blog.

    #46166. Hackathon Success Metrics That Matter After Demo Day

    📅 19 Nov 2026 • ⏱️ 7m • 📚 Deep Dive (1330 w)
    📖 Baca
    General 📈 Bullish 🌐 Dev ↗ Open Full Page

    Hackathon Success Metrics That Matter After Demo Day

    📅 19 Nov 2026 | ⏱️ 7 min read (1330 words, 📚 Deep Dive) | Source: Dev

    ⏱️ ~7 mins left to finish
    📖 0% read
    💡 Key Takeaways
    • TL;DR: A buyer's checklist for measuring hackathon success: unique participants, judged projects, university reach, and post-program status instead of attendance counts.
    • A unique participant is one identified person who actually built during the program.
    • It has been revealed that you are writing the RFP.
    📑 Quick Jump: 1. Overview • 2. Key Details • 3. Closing Notes

    Originally published at mobil3.xyz.

    TL;DR: A buyer's checklist for measuring hackathon success: unique participants, judged projects, university reach, and post-program status instead of attendance counts.

    A unique participant is one identified person who actually built during the program. A judged project is a submission scored against a rubric published before the event. Post-program status is where each team stands thirty days later: still building, paused, or dissolved. These three terms carry this whole article.

    It has been revealed that you are writing the RFP. Or you already signed one, the weekend ran, the photos look great, and your CFO asks what the company got for the spend. If the vendor's answer starts with how many people revealed up, you have learned almost nothing about whether the money worked.

    Industry observers note that attendance is the easiest number in the industry to produce and the hardest to defend. It measures logistics, not outcomes. The research on what actually happens to hackathon projects after demo day is blunt, and any buyer who reads it will stop treating a full room as evidence of anything.

    The most cited academic work on hackathon sustainability followed projects from public hackathons and found that around 65% showed no continued activity after the event ended, and that only about 3.55% were still active five months later (Nolte, Chounta, and Herbsleb, ACM CSCW 2020). A literature review of hackathon outcomes agrees: results are real but uneven, and rarely measured after the weekend (Medina et al., 2020).

    According to recent reports, so what does this mean for a buyer? Read the findings together. A packed venue tells you recruitment worked. It claims nothing about whether anything was built that survives Monday morning. When most output goes dark by design, turnout cannot tell you whether the program produced value. What does? The five metrics below.

    There is also a conversion gap on the way in. Devpost's own published guidance puts registrant-to-active-builder conversion somewhere between 5% and 33% depending on the event (Devpost hackathon handbook). A thousand registrations can mean three hundred builders or fifty. Registrations are intent. Builders are the resource you paid to convene.

    None of this means hackathons are a bad buy. It means the measurement has to be specified up front, because nobody volunteers it afterward. Research on corporate hackathons notes plainly that return on investment is hard to establish and depends entirely on objectives being defined before the event runs (Roy and Laskowski, 2017).

    According to recent reports, ask for deduplicated individuals who built something during the program. One person who attends in two cities and registers twice is still one participant. Counting method matters as much as the count itself. If a vendor cannot explain their deduplication method, treat their other numbers with suspicion.

    Recent findings suggest that registrations still have a use, but only as a ratio denominator. Registrations divided by unique builders is a recruitment-quality metric. A smaller room where most people built beats a huge room where most people watched.

    A project that was not judged against criteria published before the event is a demo, not an outcome. The rubric is what makes the count defensible. Public frameworks like Major League Hacking's judging guidance and university-published rubrics such as the one from Claremont Graduate University give sponsors an external reference point, so the bar was set before anyone wrote a line of code.

    According to recent reports, ask for three numbers here: projects submitted, projects judged complete against the rubric, and projects that scored above the quality threshold you agreed on. The third number is the one that predicts whether anything continues.

    Sources indicate that what counts as reach? Named institutions among actual builders. Not flyers. Not club contacts. In Mexico this matters more than in most markets. Campus communities are where many working developers first touch a company's stack. GitHub's Octoverse 2024 put registered developers in Mexico at around 1.9 million, growing about 21% year over year (GitHub Octoverse 2024). A program that can name fifteen institutions it drew builders from has produced a recruiting map. A program that cannot name five has produced an email list.

    Judge quality is a proxy for what the scores mean. A rubric applied by senior engineers from the sponsoring tech giant produces signal: interview lists, follow-up challenges. A rubric applied by whoever was available produces noise. Ask for the judge roster with roles, and ask whether submissions were anonymized. Both questions take thirty seconds. They belong in the package review too when you sponsor a hackathon in Mexico.

    It has been revealed that almost nobody reports this metric, and it addresses the 65% problem directly. Thirty days after demo day, every team answers one question: are you still building? Answers sort into still building, paused, and dissolved. Each team still going becomes a concrete follow-up candidate for hiring, grants, or a pilot. Against the research baseline, even modest continuation stands out.

    To be clear, turnout is not worthless. It is evidence about one thing: whether recruitment worked. Check-in totals, session fill rates, and no-show rates tell you whether your recruiting channels reached real people. In our own programs, cumulative check-ins across sessions have served exactly this role, as a supporting row in the operations section of a report rather than its headline. The same discipline applies to press mentions: they prove the story traveled, not that anything got built.

    The test is simple. Take any attendance-style figure out of a report. If nothing important remains, the report was measuring logistics. If the five metrics above remain, the report was measuring outcomes.

    Industry observers note that specify the deliverable before signing. A defensible post-program report has six sections:.

    Industry observers note that how do you spot a good vendor fast? Vendors who operate this way send a sample report the same week. Vendors who resist have told you something useful.

    Recent findings suggest that what do you ask first? Unique participants, not registrations. Then judged projects, not photo counts. Then university reach among actual builders. Then the judge roster. Then 30-day status.

    What do you ignore? Raw registrations. Press counts used as proof of building. Survey scores with no response count. Promises of conversion funnels after the fact.

    According to recent reports, why this order? Because each item is cheap to verify and hard to fake. A vendor who can answer all five already runs a real program. A vendor who cannot is selling a weekend.

    In a recent development, mobil3 designs and runs hackathons and innovation challenges in Mexico and Latin America, and reports every program against the format described above: unique participants, judged projects, university reach, and post-program status. If you are writing a hackathon into an RFP, see our sample report structure. Leave us your details on the contact page or write to ian@mobil3.xyz.

    Recent findings suggest that this guide was written by Ian Lee, founder of Mobil3, from direct program operations across Mexico. For questions about this article or our editorial process, contact us at hello@mobil3.xyz or read more about us. For the operator side of running these programs, read how to run a developer hackathon. Related: developer adoption as a program and working with universities in Mexico.

    How do you measure hackathon success?

    According to recent reports, measure unique participants, projects submitted to a published judging rubric, university reach, judge quality, and post-program status at 30 days. Attendance is a supporting number, not the outcome.

    According to recent reports, partially. Research reveals most hackathon projects go dark within months, so honest measurement focuses on what survived: continued builds, hiring conversations, and a written report a sponsor can defend internally.

    What should a sponsor report include after a hackathon?

    Unique participant count, judged project count against a published rubric, university and institution reach, judge roster, budget versus plan, and a 30-day follow-up on which teams kept building.

    Have you run or joined a program like this? Tell us in the comments what worked and what did not.

    This Breakfast Addition Sharpens Memory Later In The Day

    📅 29 Oct 2026 | ⏱️ 3 min read (547 words, 📚 Deep Dive) | Source: Org

    ⏱️ ~3 mins left to finish
    📖 0% read
    💡 Key Takeaways
    • A simple breakfast addition improved reaction times, but its effects on memory took a more complicated turn.
    • A simple breakfast addition improved reaction times, but its effects on memory took a more complicated turn.
    • Adding walnuts to breakfast could help people respond faster on mental tasks and learn information more effectively later in the day.
    📑 Quick Jump: 1. Overview • 2. Key Details • 3. Closing Notes

    A simple breakfast addition improved reaction times, but its effects on memory took a more complicated turn.

    A simple breakfast addition improved reaction times, but its effects on memory took a more complicated turn.

    Adding walnuts to breakfast could help people respond faster on mental tasks and learn information more effectively later in the day.

    A generous handful produced small cognitive benefits over the following six hours, although memory performance varied with the timing of the tests.

    Walnuts may influence how the brain directs attention and obtains the energy needed for demanding mental work.

    Professor Claire Williams, study co-author, remarked:.

    “A handful of walnuts with breakfast could give young adults a mental edge when they need to perform at the top of their game.”.

    The research involved over 30 healthy young adults aged 18–30, who ate two different breakfasts on separate visits to the laboratory.

    One contained 50 g of crushed walnuts mixed into muesli and vanilla yoghurt, while the other contained no nuts.

    The breakfasts contained almost identical calorie and fat totals, with butter added to the comparison meal to help achieve this match.

    Participants completed tests before breakfast and again two, four and six hours afterwards, while researchers also recorded their brain activity.

    After the walnut breakfast, participants responded faster on tasks involving attention, resisting distractions and switching between different mental rules.

    These abilities form part of executive function, which helps us control our responses and adapt to changing demands.

    The differences were modest, averaging around eight milliseconds on the attention test and 22 milliseconds when switching between rules.

    Whether improvements of this size would make a noticeable difference outside the laboratory remains uncertain.

    The memory findings were more complicated.

    Two hours after eating walnuts, participants performed slightly worse when repeatedly learning and recalling a list of words.

    By six hours, however, the pattern had reversed, with better performance after walnuts than after the comparison breakfast.

    One possibility is that walnuts helped protect learning performance as the testing day wore on.

    Repeated mental effort can make it harder to take in newly introduced information, so preserving the ability to learn could be useful even without improving every aspect of memory.

    However, participants did not report feeling less mentally fatigued after walnuts, leaving this explanation unconfirmed.

    Another possibility is that some benefits emerged gradually as nutrients were absorbed and processed.

    Walnuts contain omega-3 fats, protein and plant compounds called polyphenols, which could contribute individually or together.

    Electrical recordings revealed differences in frontal and parietal brain activity after the two breakfasts.

    These regions contribute to attention, memory and the control of behaviour.

    The changes may indicate that walnuts altered how mental resources were allocated during the tests, although they do not establish precisely why performance improved.

    Blood samples also revealed slightly higher glucose availability and lower concentrations of circulating free fatty acids after walnuts.

    Greater glucose availability might help fuel demanding mental work.

    The study was published in the journal Food & Function (Bell et al., 2025).

    Psychologist, Jeremy Dean, PhD is the founder and author of PsyBlog. He holds a doctorate in psychology from University College London and two other advanced degrees in psychology. He has been writing about scientific research on PsyBlog since 2004. View all posts by Dr Jeremy Dean.

    TOP 11 AI MARKETING TOOLS YOU SHOULD USE (Updated 2022)

    📅 13 Jul 2022 | ⏱️ 5 min read (973 words, 📚 Deep Dive) | Source: Blogspot

    ⏱️ ~5 mins left to finish
    📖 0% read
    💡 Key Takeaways
    • If you’re late to the AI party, don’t worry.
    • Recent findings suggest that personalize is an AI-powered technology that helps you identify and produce highly targeted sales and marketing campaigns by tracking the products and services your contacts are most interested in at any given time.
    • Seventh Sense provides behavioral analytics that helps you win attention in your customers’ overcrowded email inboxes.
    📑 Quick Jump: 1. Overview • 2. Key Details • 3. Closing Notes

    If you’re late to the AI party, don’t worry. It’s easier than you think to start leveraging artificial intelligence tools in your marketing strategy. Here are 11 AI marketing tools every marketer should start using today.

    Recent findings suggest that personalize is an AI-powered technology that helps you identify and produce highly targeted sales and marketing campaigns by tracking the products and services your contacts are most interested in at any given time. The platform uses an algorithm to identify each contact’s top three interests, which are updated in real-time based on recent site activity.

    Seventh Sense provides behavioral analytics that helps you win attention in your customers’ overcrowded email inboxes. Choosing the best day and time to send an email is always a gamble. And while some days of the week generally get higher open rates than others, you’ll never be able to nail down a time that’s best for every customer. Seventh Sense eases your stress of having to figure out the perfect send-time and day for your email campaigns. The AI-based platform figures out the best timing and email frequency for each contact based on when they’re opening emails. The tool is primarily geared toward HubSpot and Marketo customers.

    Phrasee uses artificial intelligence to help you write more effective subject lines. With its AI-based Natural Language Generation system, Phrasee uses data-driven insights to generate millions of natural-sounding copy variants that match your brand voice. The model is end-to-end, meaning when you feed the results back to Phrasee, the prediction model rebuilds so it can continuously learn from your audience.

    According to recent reports, hubSpot Search Engine Optimization (SEO) is an integral tool for the Human Content team. It uses machine learning to determine how search engines understand and categorize your content. HubSpot SEO helps you improve your search engine rankings and outrank your competitors. Search engines reward websites that organize their content around core subjects, or topic clusters. HubSpot SEO helps you discover and rank for the topics that matter to your business and customers.

    When you’re limited to testing two variables against each other at a time, it can take months to get the results you’re looking for. Evolv AI lets you test all your ideas at once. It uses advanced algorithms to identify the top-performing concepts, combine them with each other, and repeat the process to achieve the best site experience.

    Sources indicate that acrolinx is a content alignment platform that helps brands scale and improves the quality of their content. It’s geared toward enterprises – its major customers include significant brands like Google, Adobe, and Amazon - to help them scale their writing efforts. Instead of spending time chasing down and fixing typos in multiple places throughout an article or blog post, you can use Acrolinx to do it all right there in one place. You start by setting your preferences for style, grammar, tone of voice, and manufacturer-specific word usage. Then, Acrolinx checks and scores your existing content to find what’s working and suggest areas for improvement. The platform provides real-time guidance and suggestions to make writing better and strengthen weak pages.

    Industry observers note that marketMuse uses an algorithm to help marketers build content strategies. The tool shows you where to target keywords to rank in specific topic categories, and recommends keywords you should go after if you want to own particular topics. It also identifies gaps and opportunities for fresh content and prioritizes them by their probable impact on your rankings. The algorithm compares your content with thousands of articles related to the same topic to uncover what’s missing from your site.

    Copilot is a suite of tools that help eCommerce businesses maintain real-time communication with customers around the clock at every stage of the funnel. Promote products, recover shopping carts and send updates or reminders directly through Messenger.

    In a recent development, yotpo’s deep learning technology evaluates your customers’ product reviews to help you make better business decisions. It identifies key topics that customers mention related to your products—and their feelings toward them. The AI engine extracts relevant reviews from past buyers and presents them in smart displays to convert new shoppers. Yotpo also saves you time moderating reviews. The AI-powered moderation tool automatically assigns a score to each review and flags reviews with negative sentiment so you can focus on quality control instead of manually reviewing every post.

    Albert is a self-learning software that automates the creation of marketing campaigns for your brand. It analyzes vast amounts of data to run optimized campaigns autonomously, allowing you to feed in your own creative content and target markets, and then use data from its database to determine key characteristics of a serious buyer. Albert identifies potential customers that match those traits, and runs trial campaigns on a small group of customers—with results refined by Albert himself—before launching it on a larger scale.

    According to recent reports, albert plugs into your existing marketing technology stack, so you still have access to your accounts, ads, search, social media, and more. Albert maps tracking and attribution to your source of truth so you can determine which channels are driving your business.

    Recent findings suggest that there are many tools and companies out there that offer AI tools, but this is a small list of resources that we have found to be helpful. If you have any other suggestions, feel free to share them in the comments below this article. As marketing evolves at such a rapid pace, latest marketing strategies will be invented that we haven't even dreamed of yet. But for now, this list should give you a good starting point on your way to implementing AI into your marketing mix.
